sources.title: UK GDPR Article 4 - Definitions
sources.summary: Defines the core terms of the UK GDPR, including personal data, processing, controller, processor, consent, personal data breach and data concerning health, together with references to the 2018 Act, domestic law and the Commissioner.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 5 - Principles relating to processing of personal data
sources.summary: Sets the principles for processing personal data: lawfulness, fairness and transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation and integrity and confidentiality. The controller is responsible for compliance with these principles and must be able to demonstrate it.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 6 - Lawfulness of processing
sources.summary: Processing is lawful only where at least one listed basis applies, including consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, a recognised legitimate interest under Annex 1 or legitimate interests not overridden by the data subject's rights, particularly where the data subject is a child.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 7 - Conditions for consent
sources.summary: Where processing relies on consent, the controller must be able to demonstrate it, a written request must be clearly distinguishable and in plain language, and withdrawal must be as easy as giving consent. Making a service conditional on unnecessary consent counts against consent being freely given.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 9 - Processing of special categories of personal data
sources.summary: Prohibits processing of special category data, such as health, ethnic origin, sex life or sexual orientation and biometric data, unless the processing has an Article 6 basis and one of the listed conditions applies, such as explicit consent, health or social care purposes or substantial public interest.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 12 - Transparent information
sources.summary: The controller must give privacy information and communications about data subject rights in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form using clear and plain language, especially for children, and must facilitate the exercise of those rights, act within the applicable time period and generally do so free of charge.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 12A - Time limits for responding to requests by data subjects
sources.summary: The time for responding to a data subject request is one month from the latest of receipt of the request, of any requested identifying information or of any fee. The controller may extend it by two further months for complex or numerous requests by giving reasoned notice within the first month.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 13 - Information when personal data are collected from the data subject
sources.summary: When personal data are collected from the data subject, the controller must provide at that time its identity and contact details, the purposes and legal basis, the recipients, any transfers, the retention period, the data subject's rights and other information listed in the article.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 14 - Information when personal data have not been obtained from the data subject
sources.summary: When personal data are obtained from someone other than the data subject, the controller must give the data subject the listed information, including the purposes, legal basis, categories of data, recipients, retention period, rights and the source of the data, within the time limits the article sets, subject to stated exceptions.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 15 - Right of access by the data subject
sources.summary: Gives the data subject the right to confirmation of whether their personal data are processed and, if so, access to the data and information such as the purposes, recipients, retention period and source. The controller must supply a copy, and the search need only be reasonable and proportionate.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 16 - Right to rectification
sources.summary: Gives the data subject the right to have inaccurate personal data about them rectified without undue delay and to have incomplete personal data completed, including by a supplementary statement.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 17 - Right to erasure
sources.summary: Gives the data subject the right to erasure of their personal data without undue delay on listed grounds, such as the data no longer being necessary, withdrawal of consent or a successful objection, subject to exceptions such as legal obligations and legal claims.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 18 - Right to restriction of processing
sources.summary: Gives the data subject the right to restrict processing where accuracy is contested, the processing is unlawful, the data are needed for legal claims or an objection is pending. Restricted data may then be processed only on limited grounds, and the data subject must be told before a restriction is lifted.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 19 - Notification obligation
sources.summary: The controller must tell each recipient of the personal data about any rectification, erasure or restriction, unless this proves impossible or involves disproportionate effort, and must tell the data subject about those recipients on request.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 20 - Right to data portability
sources.summary: Where processing is automated and based on consent or contract, the data subject may receive the personal data they provided in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format and have it transmitted to another controller, directly where technically feasible.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 21 - Right to object
sources.summary: Gives the data subject the right to object to processing based on public task or legitimate interests, which must then stop unless the controller shows compelling legitimate grounds. An objection to direct marketing, including related profiling, is absolute and the data must no longer be processed for that purpose.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 22 - Automated individual decision-making
sources.summary: Article 22 on automated individual decision-making, including profiling, was replaced by Articles 22A to 22D by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, fully in force from 5 February 2026. The corpus text holds only the amendment notes.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 25 - Data protection by design and by default
sources.summary: The controller must implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, such as pseudonymisation, to apply the data protection principles effectively, and must by default process only the personal data necessary for each purpose. Online services likely to be accessed by children must take account of children's higher protection matters.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 30 - Records of processing activities
sources.summary: Each controller and processor must keep a written record of its processing activities, covering items such as purposes, categories of data subjects and data, recipients, transfers, retention periods and security measures, and make it available to the Commissioner on request, with a limited exemption for organisations with fewer than 250 employees.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 32 - Security of processing
sources.summary: The controller and processor must implement technical and organisational measures that ensure security appropriate to the risk, including as appropriate pseudonymisation and encryption, ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience, timely restoration after an incident and regular testing of those measures.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 33 - Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority
sources.summary: The controller must notify a personal data breach to the Commissioner without undue delay and where feasible within 72 hours, unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals. Processors must notify the controller, and the controller must document every breach.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 34 - Communication of a personal data breach to the data subject
sources.summary: Where a personal data breach is likely to result in a high risk to individuals, the controller must tell the affected data subjects without undue delay in clear and plain language, unless a listed condition applies, such as the data being made unintelligible by encryption.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 35 - Data protection impact assessment
sources.summary: Before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to individuals, particularly using new technologies, the controller must carry out a data protection impact assessment describing the processing, its necessity and proportionality, the risks and the measures to address them.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 36 - Prior consultation
sources.summary: The controller must consult the Commissioner before processing where a data protection impact assessment shows a high risk that the controller has not mitigated. The Commissioner gives written advice within up to eight weeks, which may be extended by six weeks.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 44 - General principle for transfers
sources.summary: Article 44, the general principle for transfers of personal data to third countries or international organisations, was omitted from 5 February 2026 by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. The corpus text holds only the amendment note.

sources.title: DPA 2018 section 10 - Special categories of personal data
sources.summary: Processing of special category data relying on Article 9(2)(b), (h), (i) or (j) must meet a condition in Part 1 of Schedule 1, and processing relying on Article 9(2)(g) must meet a condition in Part 2. Criminal offence data processing must meet a condition in Part 1, 2 or 3.

sources.title: DPA 2018 section 14 - Automated decision-making authorised by law
sources.summary: Section 14, which set safeguards for automated decision-making authorised by law, was omitted from 5 February 2026 by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. The corpus text holds only the amendment notes.

sources.title: DPA 2018 section 21 - Definitions
sources.summary: Defines terms for Part 2 Chapter 3 of the Act, including FOI public authority, and sets when personal data count as held by such an authority by reference to the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and the Freedom of Information (Scotland) Act 2002.

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 1 paragraph 18 - Safeguarding of children and of individuals at risk
sources.summary: Sets a substantial public interest condition for processing to protect a child or an adult at risk from neglect or physical, mental or emotional harm, where consent cannot be given, cannot reasonably be obtained or would prejudice that protection.

sources.title: PECR regulation 6 - Confidentiality of communications
sources.summary: A person must not store information, or gain access to information stored, in a subscriber's or user's terminal equipment, including by instigating it or collecting information the device emits automatically, except as Schedule A1 allows.

sources.title: PECR Schedule A1 paragraph 4 - Storage or access strictly necessary to provide an information society service
sources.summary: The strict-necessity exception for cookies and other browser storage used for a requested online service, including automatic authentication and saved website choices.

sources.title: PECR regulation 22 - Use of electronic mail for direct marketing
sources.summary: A person may only send or instigate unsolicited direct marketing email to individual subscribers with the recipient's prior consent. Exceptions cover similar products and services to existing customers and charities furthering their charitable purposes, where a simple free means of refusal was given at collection and in each message.

sources.title: PECR regulation 23 - Restriction on use of automated calling systems
sources.summary: Direct marketing by electronic mail is prohibited where the sender's identity is disguised or concealed, where no valid address is given for the recipient to ask for such messages to stop and where the message breaches or promotes websites that breach regulation 7 of the Electronic Commerce Regulations 2002.

sources.title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 section 1
sources.summary: Part 1 of the Act gives the Secretary of State and the Treasury powers to make regulations about access to customer data and business data. The section defines business data, customer data, data holder, trader and customer for that Part.

sources.title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 section 87
sources.summary: This section makes consequential amendments that replace references to Article 89(1) of the UK GDPR with Article 84B in the UK GDPR, the Data Protection Act 2018 and Scottish mental health legislation, aligning research, archiving and statistics safeguards with the new Chapter 8A.

sources.title: Equality Act 2010 section 13 - Direct discrimination
sources.summary: A person directly discriminates against another if, because of a protected characteristic, they treat that person less favourably than they treat or would treat others. Age discrimination can be justified as a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim, and more favourable treatment of disabled persons is not discrimination against a non-disabled person.

sources.title: Equality Act 2010 section 19 - Indirect discrimination
sources.summary: Indirect discrimination occurs when a provision, criterion or practice applied to everyone puts people sharing a protected characteristic at a particular disadvantage, puts the individual at that disadvantage and cannot be shown to be a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim.

sources.title: Equality Act 2010 section 6 - Disability
sources.summary: A person has a disability if they have a physical or mental impairment with a substantial and long-term adverse effect on their ability to carry out normal day-to-day activities. The Act also applies to people who have had a disability, and Schedule 1 supplements the definition.

sources.title: Equality Act 2010 Schedule 1 - Disability: supplementary provision
sources.summary: Schedule 1 supplements the definition of disability: an effect is long-term if it has lasted or is likely to last 12 months or for life, treated impairments are assessed as if untreated, and cancer, HIV infection and multiple sclerosis are each a disability. It also sets the procedure for statutory guidance on the definition.

sources.title: Equality Act 2010 section 20 - Duty to make adjustments
sources.summary: The duty to make reasonable adjustments has three requirements: to take reasonable steps to avoid substantial disadvantage to disabled persons caused by a provision, criterion or practice, by a physical feature or by the absence of an auxiliary aid. Information must be provided in an accessible format where reasonable, and the disabled person cannot be charged for the adjustments.

sources.title: Equality Act 2010 section 21 - Failure to comply with duty
sources.summary: Failing to comply with any of the three requirements of the duty to make reasonable adjustments is a failure to comply with that duty, and a person who fails to comply with it in relation to a disabled person discriminates against that person.

sources.title: Equality Act 2010 section 29 - Provision of services, etc.
sources.summary: A service-provider must not discriminate against, harass or victimise a person by refusing the service, in its terms, by ending it or by any other detriment. Service-providers and persons exercising public functions are subject to the duty to make reasonable adjustments.

sources.title: Equality Act 2010 Schedule 2 - Services and public functions: reasonable adjustments
sources.summary: Where a service-provider has the duty to make reasonable adjustments, it must comply with all three requirements in relation to disabled persons generally, and may adopt a reasonable alternative method of providing the service. It need not take a step that would fundamentally alter the nature of the service or its trade, and special rules apply to transport vehicles.

sources.title: Consumer Rights Act 2015 section 49 - Service to be performed with reasonable care and skill
sources.summary: Every contract to supply a service is treated as including a term that the trader must perform the service with reasonable care and skill. Section 54 sets out the consumer's rights if the trader breaches that term.

sources.title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 section 225 - Prohibition of unfair commercial practices
sources.summary: Unfair commercial practices are prohibited, including their promotion through a code of conduct. A practice is unfair if it involves a misleading action or omission, an aggressive practice or a breach of professional diligence likely to change the average consumer's transactional decision; it is also unfair if it omits material information from an invitation to purchase or is listed in Schedule 20.

sources.title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 Schedule 20 - Commercial practices which are in all circumstances considered unfair
sources.summary: Schedule 20 lists 32 commercial practices that are unfair in all circumstances. They include displaying a trust mark without authorisation, submitting or commissioning fake or concealed incentivised reviews, publishing reviews misleadingly, falsely claiming a product can treat disease and describing a product as free when the consumer must pay.

sources.title: CMA208 - Fake reviews: guidance on the prohibition under paragraph 13 of Schedule 20 to the DMCC Act 2024
sources.summary: CMA guidance on paragraph 13 of Schedule 20 to the DMCC Act 2024 states that publishing consumer reviews or review information in a misleading way is prohibited. Traders should not suppress genuine negative reviews, cherry-pick positive ones or display ratings that ignore removed fake reviews or that are influenced by commissions.

sources.title: Personal data breaches: a guide
sources.summary: ICO guidance explains that a notifiable personal data breach must be reported to the ICO without undue delay and within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, and that individuals must be told without undue delay where the breach is likely to result in a high risk to them. All breaches must be documented, whether or not they are reported.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 26 - Joint controllers
sources.summary: Where two or more controllers jointly determine the purposes and means of processing, they are joint controllers and must set out their respective responsibilities in a transparent arrangement. The essence of the arrangement must be available to data subjects, who may exercise their rights against each controller.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 28 - Processor
sources.summary: A controller may only use processors that give sufficient guarantees of appropriate measures, under a written contract setting out the processing and requiring the processor to act on documented instructions, keep data confidential and secure, assist the controller, delete or return data at the end and allow audits. Sub-processors need the controller's authorisation and the same obligations.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 22A - Automated processing and significant decisions
sources.summary: A decision is based solely on automated processing if there is no meaningful human involvement in taking it, and it is a significant decision if it produces a legal or similarly significant effect for the data subject. Assessing meaningful human involvement must consider the extent to which the decision relies on profiling.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 22B - Restrictions on automated decision-making
sources.summary: A significant decision based solely on automated processing may not rely on special category data unless the data subject gave explicit consent or the decision is necessary for a contract or required or authorised by law and Article 9(2)(g) applies. Such decisions also may not rely on processing under the recognised legitimate interests basis in Article 6(1)(ea).

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 22C - Safeguards for automated decision-making
sources.summary: Where a controller takes a significant decision based solely on automated processing of personal data, it must put safeguards in place that give the data subject information about the decision and let them make representations, obtain human intervention and contest the decision.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 22D - Further provision about automated decision-making
sources.summary: The Secretary of State may by regulations specify when there is or is not meaningful human involvement in a decision, which decisions have a similarly significant effect, and additional or supplementary requirements for automated decision-making safeguards. Such regulations may not amend Article 22C and follow the affirmative resolution procedure.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 44A - General principles for transfers
sources.summary: A controller or processor may transfer personal data to a third country or international organisation only if the transfer is approved by regulations under Article 45A, is subject to appropriate safeguards under Article 46 or relies on an Article 49 derogation, and otherwise complies with the Regulation.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 84B - Additional requirements when processing for RAS purposes
sources.summary: Personal data may be processed for research, archiving or statistical purposes only if the processing is collection, converts the data into a form that does not identify the data subject or is needed to fulfil those purposes. Such processing must be subject to appropriate safeguards for the data subject's rights and freedoms.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 8A - Purpose limitation: further processing
sources.summary: Inserted by DUAA 2025 s.71(5) (in force 19.6.2025 for specified purposes, 5.2.2026 otherwise). Sets the Article 5(1)(b) compatibility test for further processing: factors in para 2, deemed-compatible cases in para 3 (fresh specific consent, Article 84B research/archiving/statistics, compliance checks, Annex 2 conditions, Article 23(1) objectives), the narrower route where the original processing relied on consent (para 4), and the Secretary of State's affirmative-procedure power to amend Annex 2 (paras 5-8).

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 11 - Processing which does not require identification
sources.summary: A controller whose purposes do not or no longer require identifying a data subject need not keep or acquire extra information only to comply with the Regulation. Where it can show it cannot identify the data subject, it informs them if possible, and Articles 15 to 20 do not apply unless the data subject supplies identifying information.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 84A - Research, archives and statistics
sources.summary: Opens Chapter 8A (inserted by DUAA 2025 s.86(2), in force 19.6.2025 for specified purposes, 5.2.2026 otherwise), which replaces the omitted Article 89. Defines the RAS purposes the chapter governs.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 84C - Appropriate safeguards
sources.summary: When the Article 84B(2) requirement for appropriate safeguards is met for research, archiving or statistical processing: technical and organisational measures respecting data minimisation (including pseudonymisation), no measures or decisions about particular data subjects outside approved medical research, and no substantial damage or distress. Successor to omitted Article 89(1).

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 84D - Appropriate safeguards: further provision
sources.summary: Secretary of State power to make regulations adding to, varying or omitting the Article 84C safeguards for research, archiving or statistical processing.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 89 - Safeguards and derogations relating to processing for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes
sources.summary: Omitted on 5.2.2026 by DUAA 2025 s.86(4) (S.I. 2026/82 reg. 2(n)). The safeguards now sit in Chapter 8A, Articles 84A to 84D; cite those for current law. Kept so that citations of Article 89(1) in older guidance resolve to a record of the omission.

sources.title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 Commencement No. 6 Regulations 2026 regulation 5 - Saving provision
sources.summary: The automated decision-making amendments made by section 80 of and Schedule 6 to the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 do not apply to decisions taken before 5 February 2026 to which the previous Article 22(3) UK GDPR or sections 14(1) or 50(2) of the Data Protection Act 2018 applied.

sources.title: EU GDPR Article 3 - Territorial scope
sources.summary: The EU GDPR applies to processing in the context of an EU establishment wherever it takes place, and to processing by controllers or processors outside the EU of personal data of people in the EU where it relates to offering them goods or services or monitoring their behaviour in the EU.

sources.title: EU GDPR Article 27 - Representatives of controllers or processors not established in the Union
sources.summary: A controller or processor outside the EU that is caught by Article 3(2) must designate in writing a representative established in a Member State where relevant data subjects are. The duty does not apply to occasional low-risk processing without large-scale special category or criminal offence data, or to public bodies.

sources.title: EU GDPR Article 77 - Right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority
sources.summary: Every data subject has the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority, in particular in the Member State of their habitual residence, place of work or the alleged infringement. The authority must inform the complainant of the progress and outcome, including the possibility of a judicial remedy.

sources.title: EU AI Act Article 3 - Definitions
sources.summary: Article 3 sets out the definitions used throughout the EU AI Act, including AI system, risk, provider, deployer, authorised representative, importer, distributor, operator and placing on the market.

sources.title: EU AI Act Article 5 - Prohibited AI practices
sources.summary: Prohibits placing on the market or using AI systems for listed practices, including manipulative or subliminal techniques, exploiting vulnerabilities due to age, disability or social situation, social scoring, emotion recognition at work or school and certain biometric categorisation and identification uses.

sources.title: EU AI Act Article 50 - Transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems
sources.summary: Requires providers to inform people when they interact with an AI system and to mark synthetic audio, image, video or text output as artificially generated. Deployers must disclose emotion recognition, biometric categorisation and deep fake content.

sources.title: EU AI Act Article 2 - Scope
sources.summary: Original text as published in the Official Journal; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 Article 1 amends it. Covers third-country providers and deployers where the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union; this is the route by which a provider or deployer outside the Union comes into scope.

sources.title: EU AI Act Article 4 - AI literacy
sources.summary: Original AI literacy duty for providers and deployers. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 Article 1 replaces it with a duty to take measures supporting AI literacy; read the two together.

sources.title: EU AI Act Article 6 - Classification rules for high-risk AI systems
sources.summary: An Annex III system is high-risk unless it poses no significant risk of harm under the paragraph 3 conditions; one that profiles natural persons is always high-risk.

sources.title: EU AI Act Article 113 - Entry into force and application
sources.summary: Original application dates, from 2 August 2026 with staggered exceptions. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 changes the high-risk dates; read its Article 1 and Article 4 before citing any date.

sources.title: EU AI Act Annex III - High-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2)
sources.summary: The high-risk use-case list. Point 1(b) covers biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes; point 4(a) and 4(b) cover recruitment, selection and decisions on work relationships, which the draft Article 6(5) guidelines read onto ranking self-employed service providers.

sources.title: Digital Omnibus on AI Article 1 - Amendments to Regulation (EU) 2024/1689
sources.summary: The point-by-point amendments to the AI Act, including Articles 2, 4, 50 and 113 and the high-risk timetable. No consolidated AI Act text exists yet, so the original articles must be read with this one.

sources.title: Digital Omnibus on AI Article 4 - Entry into force and application
sources.summary: When the Digital Omnibus amendments take effect.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 3 - General interpretation
sources.summary: Sets out the general definitions used throughout the Money Laundering Regulations 2017, such as authorised person, beneficial owner, the FCA and other key terms, often by reference to other regulations.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 4 - Meaning of business relationship
sources.summary: Defines a business relationship as a business, professional or commercial relationship arising from the relevant person's business that is expected to have an element of duration, with specific rules for certain services and estate agents.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 7 - Supervisory authorities
sources.summary: Names the supervisory authorities for relevant persons, including the FCA for credit and financial institutions and cryptoasset businesses, the listed professional bodies for their members and HMRC for high value dealers and other businesses.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 8 - Application
sources.summary: Applies the Regulations to relevant persons acting in the course of business in the United Kingdom, listing credit and financial institutions, accountants, legal professionals, estate agents, high value dealers, casinos, art market participants and cryptoasset businesses.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 18 - Risk assessment by relevant persons
sources.summary: Requires a relevant person to identify and assess the money laundering and terrorist financing risks to its business, taking account of customers, geography, products, transactions and delivery channels, and to keep a written record of the steps taken.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 18A - Risk assessment by relevant persons in relation to proliferation financing
sources.summary: Requires a relevant person to identify and assess the proliferation financing risks to its business, considering the Treasury risk assessment and listed risk factors, and to keep an up-to-date written record of the steps taken.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 19 - Policies, controls and procedures
sources.summary: Requires a relevant person to establish, review and record proportionate policies, controls and procedures approved by senior management to mitigate the money laundering and terrorist financing risks identified in its risk assessment.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 21 - Internal controls
sources.summary: Requires a relevant person, where appropriate to its size and nature, to appoint a senior officer responsible for compliance, screen relevant employees and establish an independent audit function to evaluate its policies and controls.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 24 - Training
sources.summary: Requires a relevant person to make relevant employees and agents aware of the law on money laundering, terrorist financing, proliferation financing and data protection, give them regular training and keep a written record of the measures taken.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 26 - Prohibitions and approvals
sources.summary: Prohibits a person from being a beneficial owner, officer or manager of certain firms, such as accountants, legal professionals, estate agents and high value dealers, without approval from the firm's supervisory authority.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 27 - Customer due diligence
sources.summary: Requires a relevant person to apply customer due diligence when establishing a business relationship, carrying out certain occasional transactions above set thresholds, suspecting money laundering or terrorist financing, or doubting earlier identification information.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 28 - Customer due diligence measures
sources.summary: Sets out the customer due diligence measures, requiring a relevant person to identify and verify the customer and any beneficial owner and to assess the purpose and intended nature of the business relationship or transaction.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 33 - Obligation to apply enhanced customer due diligence
sources.summary: Requires a relevant person to apply enhanced customer due diligence and enhanced ongoing monitoring in high-risk cases, including relationships with high-risk third countries, correspondent relationships and politically exposed persons.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 35 - Enhanced customer due diligence: politically exposed persons
sources.summary: Requires a relevant person to have risk-management systems to identify politically exposed persons, their family members and known close associates, and to apply enhanced measures such as senior approval and establishing the source of wealth and funds.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 37 - Application of simplified customer due diligence
sources.summary: Permits a relevant person to apply simplified customer due diligence where it determines that a business relationship or transaction presents a low risk, while it continues to meet core requirements and monitors for unusual or suspicious transactions.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 39 - Reliance
sources.summary: Permits a relevant person to rely on specified third parties to apply customer due diligence measures, but the relevant person remains liable for any failure and must obtain the information and arrange access to copies of the documents.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 40 - Record-keeping
sources.summary: Requires a relevant person to keep copies of customer due diligence documents and supporting transaction records for a specified period, after which personal data must be deleted unless an exception applies.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 41 - Data protection
sources.summary: Restricts personal data obtained under the Regulations to the purposes of preventing money laundering, terrorist financing or proliferation financing unless another enactment permits other use or the data subject consents, and requires a statement to new customers.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 54 - Duty to maintain registers of certain relevant persons
sources.summary: Requires the FCA and HMRC to maintain registers of certain relevant persons, including money service businesses, trust or company service providers, cryptoasset businesses, high value dealers and certain payment service providers.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 55 - Power to maintain registers
sources.summary: Allows the FCA to maintain a register of Annex 1 financial institutions and HMRC to maintain registers of certain unsupervised relevant persons, such as estate agents, accountants and tax advisers, and sets how such registers are kept.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 56 - Requirement to be registered
sources.summary: Requires a person who must appear in a register maintained under regulation 54 to be registered before acting as a high value dealer, money service business, trust or company service provider, payment service provider or cryptoasset business, subject to transitional exceptions.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 57 - Applications for registration in a register maintained under regulation 54 or 55
sources.summary: Requires an applicant for registration to apply in the manner the registering authority specifies, providing information such as business details, the nominated officer, a risk assessment and how the business meets its anti-money laundering obligations.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 58 - Fit and proper test
sources.summary: Requires the registering authority to refuse registration of a money service business or trust or company service provider if the applicant or its officers, managers, beneficial owners or agents are not fit and proper persons, including those convicted of listed offences.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 59 - Determination of applications for registration under regulations 54 and 55
sources.summary: Allows the registering authority to refuse registration where requirements are unmet, information is false or misleading, penalties or charges are unpaid, the supervisory authority objects or it suspects the applicant will fail to comply, and sets notification duties.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 76 - Power to impose civil penalties: fines and statements
sources.summary: Allows a designated supervisory authority to impose a penalty or publish a statement of censure on a person who contravenes a relevant requirement, and to penalise an officer knowingly concerned, unless all reasonable steps were taken.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 86 - Criminal offence
sources.summary: Makes contravention of a relevant requirement a criminal offence punishable by imprisonment of up to two years, a fine or both, with a defence for a person who took all reasonable steps and exercised due diligence.

sources.title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 regulation 92 - Offence by bodies corporate, partnership or unincorporated association
sources.summary: Makes an officer of a body corporate, partnership or unincorporated association personally guilty of an offence under this Part committed with their consent or connivance or attributable to their neglect.

sources.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 section 19 - The general prohibition
sources.summary: Prohibits any person from carrying on, or purporting to carry on, a regulated activity in the United Kingdom unless they are an authorised person or an exempt person. This is called the general prohibition.

sources.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 section 21 - Restrictions on financial promotion
sources.summary: A person must not, in the course of business, communicate an invitation or inducement to engage in investment or claims management activity unless they are an authorised person or an authorised person approves the content. A communication from outside the United Kingdom is caught only if it can have an effect in the United Kingdom.

sources.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 section 22 - Regulated activities
sources.summary: Defines a regulated activity as an activity of a kind specified by Treasury order, carried on by way of business, that relates to a specified investment, to information about a person's financial standing, to administering a benchmark or to claims management services in Great Britain.

sources.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 section 23 - Contravention of the general prohibition or section 20(1) or (1A)
sources.summary: Makes contravention of the general prohibition a criminal offence punishable by a fine, imprisonment or both. It also makes it an offence for an authorised person to carry on a credit-related regulated activity without the relevant permission.

sources.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 section 25 - Contravention of section 21
sources.summary: Makes contravention of the financial promotion restriction in section 21(1) a criminal offence punishable by a fine, imprisonment or both. It is a defence to show a reasonable belief that an authorised person prepared or approved the content, or that all reasonable precautions and due diligence were taken.

sources.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Financial Promotion) Order 2005 article 12 - Communications to overseas recipients
sources.summary: Exempts from the financial promotion restriction a communication made to a person who receives it outside the United Kingdom, or directed only at persons outside the United Kingdom. Unsolicited real time communications qualify only when made from abroad for a business carried on only outside the United Kingdom.

sources.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Financial Promotion) Order 2005 article 19 - Investment professionals
sources.summary: Exempts from the financial promotion restriction a communication made only to, or directed only at, investment professionals. It sets indicators, such as warnings and systems that stop other recipients engaging, that show a communication is directed only at investment professionals.

sources.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Financial Promotion) Order 2005 article 48 - Certified high net worth individuals
sources.summary: Exempts certain non-real time or solicited real time communications made to an individual reasonably believed to be a certified high net worth individual, who has signed a Schedule 5 statement in the last twelve months. The communication must carry the prescribed warning and information and relate only to specified investments.

sources.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Financial Promotion) Order 2005 article 49 - High net worth companies, unincorporated associations etc.
sources.summary: Exempts from the financial promotion restriction a communication made only to, or directed only at, high net worth bodies corporate, unincorporated associations, partnerships, trustees of high value trusts and their relevant directors, officers or employees, above set net asset or share capital thresholds.

sources.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Financial Promotion) Order 2005 article 50 - Sophisticated investors
sources.summary: Exempts a communication made to a certified sophisticated investor, who holds a current certificate signed by an authorised person and has signed a statement in the last twelve months. The communication must relate only to the certified investment type and carry the prescribed indications.

sources.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Financial Promotion) Order 2005 article 50A - Self-certified sophisticated investors
sources.summary: Exempts a communication made to an individual reasonably believed to be a self-certified sophisticated investor, who has signed a Schedule 5 Part 2 statement in the last twelve months. The communication must carry the prescribed warning and information and relate only to specified investments.

sources.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Financial Promotion) Order 2005 article 51 - Associations of high net worth or sophisticated investors
sources.summary: Exempts non-real time or solicited real time communications made to an association, or its members, made up wholly or mainly of high net worth or sophisticated investors, where the investment cannot create a liability beyond the amount committed. The exemption does not cover qualifying cryptoassets.

sources.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001 article 5 - Accepting deposits
sources.summary: Specifies accepting deposits as a regulated activity where deposit money is lent to others or finances the business. It defines a deposit as a repayable sum not referable to the provision of property, services or security, such as an advance payment or security deposit under a contract.

sources.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001 article 39D - Debt adjusting
sources.summary: Specifies debt adjusting as a regulated activity: negotiating terms for discharging a debt with a lender or owner on a borrower's or hirer's behalf, taking over their obligation to discharge a debt in return for payments, or similar debt liquidation activity under a credit or consumer hire agreement.

sources.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001 article 39E - Debt-counselling
sources.summary: Specifies debt-counselling as a regulated activity: giving advice to a borrower or hirer about the liquidation of a debt due under a credit agreement or a consumer hire agreement.

sources.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001 article 60B - Regulated credit agreements
sources.summary: Specifies entering into a regulated credit agreement as lender, and exercising the lender's rights and duties under one, as regulated activities. It defines a credit agreement and treats any credit agreement that is not an exempt agreement under articles 60C to 60H as regulated.

sources.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001 article 60C - Exempt agreements: exemptions relating to the nature of the agreement
sources.summary: Sets out credit agreements that are exempt because of their nature, including agreements that are regulated mortgage contracts or home purchase plans, business lending over 25,000 pounds and certain business green deal plans.

sources.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001 article 61 - Regulated mortgage contracts
sources.summary: Specifies entering into and administering a regulated mortgage contract as regulated activities. A regulated mortgage contract is credit to an individual or trustees secured by a mortgage on land of which at least 40% is used as or in connection with a dwelling.

sources.title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 section 226 - Misleading actions
sources.summary: When false or deceptive information, or a breach of a code commitment, makes a commercial practice a misleading action.

sources.title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 section 227 - Misleading omissions
sources.summary: When omitting, hiding or obscuring material information makes a commercial practice a misleading omission, and what counts as material information.

sources.title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 section 228 - Aggressive practices
sources.summary: When harassment, coercion or undue influence makes a commercial practice aggressive.

sources.title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 section 229 - Contravention of the requirements of professional diligence
sources.summary: The standard of special skill and care a trader owes consumers in its field of activity.

sources.title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 section 230 - Omission of material information from invitation to purchase
sources.summary: The listed information an invitation to purchase must carry, including the total price and the trader's identity and contact details.

sources.title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 section 245 - Meaning of transactional decision
sources.summary: The decisions by a consumer that count as transactional decisions for the unfair commercial practices prohibition.

sources.title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 section 246 - Meaning of average consumer: general
sources.summary: The average consumer benchmark against which the effect of a commercial practice is judged.

sources.title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 section 247 - Meaning of average consumer: vulnerable consumers
sources.summary: The vulnerable-consumer adjustment to the average consumer benchmark: where a practice is likely to affect a group that is particularly vulnerable to it or to the product in a way the trader could reasonably foresee, including because of their physical or mental health, the average consumer is an average member of that group.

sources.title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 section 248 - Meaning of product
sources.summary: What counts as a product, including services, digital content and rights or obligations.

sources.title: Consumer Rights Act 2015 section 62 - Requirement for contract terms and notices to be fair
sources.summary: The fairness test for consumer contract terms and notices, and the effect of an unfair term.

sources.title: Consumer Rights Act 2015 section 64 - Exclusion from assessment of fairness
sources.summary: When a term about the main subject matter or the price escapes the fairness assessment, conditional on transparency and prominence.

sources.title: Consumer Rights Act 2015 section 68 - Requirement for transparency
sources.summary: The duty to express written consumer contract terms and notices in plain and intelligible language, and legibly.

sources.title: Consumer Rights Act 2015 Schedule 2 - Consumer contract terms which may be regarded as unfair
sources.summary: The indicative grey list of consumer contract terms that may be regarded as unfair.

sources.title: Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 section 3 - Liability arising in contract
sources.summary: Where one party deals on the other's written standard terms of business, the other cannot by a contract term exclude or restrict its liability for its own breach, or claim to render a substantially different performance or none at all, except so far as the term satisfies the requirement of reasonableness. Subsection (3) excludes consumer contracts, which section 62 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 governs instead.

sources.title: Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 section 11 - The 'reasonableness' test
sources.summary: The requirement of reasonableness: a term must have been fair and reasonable to include, having regard to the circumstances known to or in the contemplation of the parties when the contract was made. Where a term limits liability to a specified sum, regard is had to the resources available to meet the liability and how far insurance could cover it, and the party relying on the term must show that it is reasonable.

sources.title: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 section 16 - The acts restricted by copyright in a work
sources.summary: The owner of copyright in a work has the exclusive right to copy it, issue copies to the public, rent or lend it, perform, show or play it in public, communicate it to the public and make an adaptation of it. Copyright is infringed by a person who, without the licence of the copyright owner, does or authorises another to do any of those acts in relation to the whole or any substantial part of the work.

sources.title: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 section 77 - Right to be identified as author or director
sources.summary: The author of a copyright literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, and the director of a copyright film, has the right to be identified as such when the work is published commercially, performed, shown or communicated to the public, and in the further cases the section lists. The identification must be clear and reasonably prominent. The right is not infringed unless it has been asserted under section 78.

sources.title: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 section 78 - Requirement that right be asserted
sources.summary: The section 77 right is not infringed unless it has been asserted, generally or in relation to a specified act, by an instrument in writing signed by the author or director, or on an assignment of copyright. A person to whom the assertion is made, or who has notice of it, is bound by it. In proceedings for infringement the court takes any delay in asserting the right into account.

sources.title: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 section 80 - Right to object to derogatory treatment of work
sources.summary: The author of a copyright literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, and the director of a copyright film, has the right not to have the work subjected to derogatory treatment. A treatment is any addition to, deletion from, alteration to or adaptation of the work, and it is derogatory if it amounts to distortion or mutilation of the work or is otherwise prejudicial to the honour or reputation of the author or director. The section lists the acts that infringe the right for each kind of work.

sources.title: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 section 87 - Consent and waiver of rights
sources.summary: It is not an infringement of the moral rights in Chapter IV to do any act to which the person entitled to the right has consented. Any of those rights may be waived by an instrument in writing signed by the person giving up the right. A waiver may relate to a specific work, works of a specified description or works generally, may be conditional or unconditional, and may be expressed to be subject to revocation.

sources.title: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 section 90 - Assignment and licences
sources.summary: Copyright is transmissible as personal or moveable property by assignment, by testamentary disposition or by operation of law. An assignment may be partial, limited to some of the acts the owner has the exclusive right to do or to part of the copyright period, and is not effective unless it is in writing signed by or on behalf of the assignor. A licence granted by a copyright owner binds every successor in title to the owner's interest, except a purchaser in good faith for valuable consideration without notice of the licence.

sources.title: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 section 296ZG - Electronic rights management information
sources.summary: Where a person knowingly and without authority removes or alters electronic rights management information associated with a copy of a copyright work, or distributes or communicates to the public copies from which it has been removed or altered, knowing or having reason to believe that this induces, enables, facilitates or conceals an infringement, the person issuing or communicating the work and the copyright owner or exclusive licensee have the same rights against that person as for an infringement of copyright. Rights management information is information that identifies the work, the author, the copyright owner or a right holder, or the terms and conditions of use of the work.

sources.title: Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008 regulation 3 - Prohibition of advertising which misleads traders
sources.summary: Advertising which is misleading is prohibited. Advertising is misleading if it deceives or is likely to deceive the traders it is addressed to or reaches and is likely to affect their economic behaviour, or injures a competitor; account is taken of its features, in particular the price or the manner in which the price is calculated and the conditions of supply. The business-to-business counterpart of the consumer misleading-action rules, so it governs marketing of paid services to traders.

sources.title: Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008 regulation 4 - Comparative advertising
sources.summary: Comparative advertising is permitted only when it is not misleading under regulation 3 or a misleading action or omission under the DMCC Act 2024, compares products meeting the same needs, objectively compares material, relevant, verifiable and representative features, which may include price, and does not confuse, denigrate, take unfair advantage of a competitor's mark or present products as imitations.

sources.title: Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 regulation 9 - Information to be provided before making an on-premises contract
sources.summary: The pre-contract information a trader must give before an on-premises consumer contract is made.

sources.title: Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 regulation 10 - Information to be provided before making an off-premises contract
sources.summary: The pre-contract information a trader must give on a durable medium before an off-premises consumer contract is made.

sources.title: Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 regulation 13 - Information to be provided before making a distance contract
sources.summary: The pre-contract information a trader must give before a distance consumer contract is made, and how it binds the contract.

sources.title: Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 regulation 19 - Offence relating to the failure to give notice of the right to cancel
sources.summary: The criminal offence a trader commits by not giving notice of the right to cancel an off-premises contract.

sources.title: Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 Schedule 1 - Information relating to on-premises contracts
sources.summary: The listed pre-contract information for on-premises contracts referred to by regulation 9(1).

sources.title: Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 Schedule 2 - Information relating to distance and off-premises contracts
sources.summary: The listed pre-contract information for distance and off-premises contracts referred to by regulations 10(1) and 13(1).

sources.title: Electronic Commerce (EC Directive) Regulations 2002 regulation 6 - General information to be provided by a person providing an information society service
sources.summary: The identifying and pricing information an online service provider must make available to recipients.

sources.title: Electronic Commerce (EC Directive) Regulations 2002 regulation 17 - Mere conduit
sources.summary: The liability shield for an intermediary that only transmits or provides access to information.

sources.title: Electronic Commerce (EC Directive) Regulations 2002 regulation 18 - Caching
sources.summary: The liability shield for automatic, intermediate and temporary storage of transmitted information.

sources.title: Electronic Commerce (EC Directive) Regulations 2002 regulation 19 - Hosting
sources.summary: The liability shield for storing information provided by a recipient of the service, and the actual-knowledge condition that removes it.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 24 - Responsibility of the controller
sources.summary: The controller's general obligation to implement, review and update measures that ensure and demonstrate that processing complies with the Regulation.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 45 - Transfers on the basis of an adequacy decision
sources.summary: Adequacy-decision transfers, omitted on 5 February 2026 by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. Mirrored so it is not cited as live; Article 45A now carries approval by regulations.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 45A - Transfers approved by regulations
sources.summary: The Secretary of State's power to approve transfers to a third country or international organisation by regulations, subject to the data protection test.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 45B - The data protection test
sources.summary: The not-materially-lower standard a third country or international organisation must meet before transfers to it are approved by regulations.

sources.title: Data Protection (Adequacy) (United States of America) Regulations 2023 regulation 2 - Interpretation
sources.summary: Definitions for the UK-US Data Bridge: the Data Privacy Framework List that the US Department of Commerce maintains, the EU-US Data Privacy Framework and its Principles, and the UK Extension to the EU-US Data Privacy Framework.

sources.title: Data Protection (Adequacy) (United States of America) Regulations 2023 regulation 3 - Adequate level of protection
sources.summary: The UK-US Data Bridge. Specifies the United States as adequate for a transfer to a person that the Data Privacy Framework List shows as participating in the UK Extension, where the data will be subject to the Framework Principles on receipt. Participation is a per-organisation fact to check at transfer time.

sources.title: Data Protection (Adequacy) (United States of America) Regulations 2023 regulation 4 - Independent supervisory authorities
sources.summary: Names the United States Federal Trade Commission and Department of Transportation as the independent supervisory authorities for the UK Extension to the EU-US Data Privacy Framework.

sources.title: Data Protection (Adequacy) (Republic of Korea) Regulations 2022 regulation 2 - Adequate level of protection
sources.summary: Specifies the Republic of Korea as adequate for a transfer to a person subject to Korea's Personal Information Protection Act.

sources.title: Data Protection (Adequacy) (Republic of Korea) Regulations 2022 regulation 3 - Independent supervisory authorities
sources.summary: Names the Personal Information Protection Commission and the Financial Services Commission as the independent supervisory authorities in the Republic of Korea.

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 21 paragraph 4 - UK GDPR: transfers approved by regulations
sources.summary: Treats a transfer to a destination specified in paragraph 5 as approved by regulations made under UK GDPR Article 45A, and lets the Secretary of State narrow or repeal that list by regulations.

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 21 paragraph 5 - Destinations treated as approved
sources.summary: The transitional adequacy list: EEA states, Gibraltar, EU institutions, and the third countries, territories, sectors and organisations covered by EU adequacy decisions in force before IP completion day.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 46 - Transfers subject to appropriate safeguards
sources.summary: The appropriate-safeguards route for a restricted transfer, listing binding corporate rules and the standard data protection clauses issued by the Commissioner under section 119A of the Data Protection Act 2018.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 47 - Transfers subject to appropriate safeguards: Binding corporate rules
sources.summary: What binding corporate rules must contain before the Commissioner approves them as appropriate safeguards for intra-group transfers.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 47A - Transfers subject to appropriate safeguards: further provision
sources.summary: The Secretary of State's power to specify standard data protection clauses and further safeguards relied on for transfers under Article 46.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 49 - Derogations for specific situations
sources.summary: The derogations, including explicit consent and contract necessity, that permit a restricted transfer where neither approval by regulations nor appropriate safeguards apply.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 49A - Restriction in the public interest
sources.summary: The Secretary of State's power to restrict transfers of a category of personal data to a third country for important reasons of public interest.

sources.title: DPA 2018 section 119A - Standard clauses for transfers to third countries etc
sources.summary: The Commissioner's power to issue standard data protection clauses for restricted transfers, which is the statutory basis of the International Data Transfer Agreement and the UK Addendum to the EU standard contractual clauses.

sources.citation: ICO contracts and liabilities between controllers and processors
sources.title: Contracts and liabilities between controllers and processors
sources.summary: What details about the processing an Article 28(3) contract must set out, the minimum required terms including processing only on the controller's documented instructions, and the point at which a processor that acts outside those instructions becomes a controller.

sources.title: EDPB Guidelines 07/2020 on the concepts of controller and processor in the GDPR
sources.summary: How to tell a controller, a joint controller and a processor apart: joint participation through common or converging decisions, no joint control for transmission between separate controllers or a shared database where each entity sets its own purposes, the two conditions for a processor (a separate entity processing on the controller's behalf, never for its own purposes) and staff under the controller's direct authority are not processors. Also how specific an Article 28(3) contract must be and the documented instructions boundary at which a processor becomes a controller. EU guidance, persuasive only in the United Kingdom.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 8 - Conditions applicable to a child's consent in relation to information society services
sources.summary: Paras 1-4 in force since 31.12.2020: child's own consent valid from age 13 (below 13 needs parental responsibility holder), controller verification duty, no disturbance to general contract law, preventive/counselling services excluded from scope. Paras 2A/2B (NEW, in force 29.4.2026): Secretary of State may move the age 13-16 by affirmative-procedure regulations.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 8ZA - Child's consent in relation to information society services: age verification
sources.summary: New article in force since 29.4.2026 (inserted by Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026 s.72). Empowers age-verification regulations for Article 8 consent; may amend data protection legislation, set exceptions/time limits, confer discretionary functions. Affirmative procedure required. Excludes preventive/counselling services (mirrors Art.8(4)). No regulations made under it yet.

sources.title: UK GDPR Annex 1 - Lawfulness of processing: recognised legitimate interests
sources.summary: New Annex in force since 5.2.2026 (Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 c.18 s.142(1) Sch.4; S.I. 2026/82 reg.2(z6) - NOT the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026). Recognised-legitimate-interest conditions for Art.6(1)(e). Paragraphs 6-8 cover safeguarding a vulnerable individual: para 6 the condition itself, para 7 defines 'safeguarding' (protecting from neglect/harm, or protecting wellbeing) and 'vulnerable individual' (under 18, OR at risk of harm and unable to self-protect because of it), para 8 individual-vs-categorical clarification.

sources.title: DPA 2018 section 11 - Special categories of personal data etc: supplementary
sources.summary: Not children-specific. s.11(1): circumstances satisfying the Art.9(3) safeguard for Art.9(2)(h) health/social-care processing (by/under responsibility of a health professional, or another person under an equivalent confidentiality duty). s.11(2): defines personal data relating to criminal convictions/offences for DPA s.10/Art.10 purposes.

sources.title: DPA 2018 section 42 - Safeguards: sensitive processing (law enforcement purposes)
sources.summary: Part 3 (law-enforcement processing) safeguard for competent authorities only: requires an appropriate policy document (retained 6 months post-cessation, producible to the ICO) plus s.61 logging. It does not apply to a controller that is not a competent authority.

sources.title: DPA 2018 section 123 - Age-appropriate design code
sources.summary: Statutory basis for the ICO Children's Code: requires the ICO to prepare an age-appropriate-design code of practice, with mandatory consultation and a duty to reflect children's differing needs by age, having regard to UNCRC obligations. Subsection (7) confirms 'information society services' excludes preventive/counselling services, cross-referencing the same carve-out as Art.8(4)/8ZA(5).

sources.title: DPA 2018 section 127 - Effect of codes issued under section 125(4)
sources.summary: Sets the legal effect of ICO codes made under ss.121-124 (including the s.123 Children's Code): breach is not directly actionable, but a code is admissible in evidence and a court/tribunal/the ICO must take a relevant in-force provision into account. The enforcement teeth behind the Children's Code.

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 1 paragraph 2 - Health or social care purposes
sources.summary: Schedule 1 Part 1 condition: processing necessary for health or social care purposes (preventive/occupational medicine, working-capacity assessment, medical diagnosis, health/social care provision or treatment, management of health/social care systems).

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Part 2 paragraph 5 - Requirement for an appropriate policy document (substantial public interest conditions)
sources.summary: Gateway provision for every Part 2 substantial-public-interest condition (paragraphs 6-28, including paragraph 18's children/vulnerable-individuals safeguarding condition, already mirrored): a Part 2 condition is only met if an appropriate policy document is in place when the processing happens. Points to Part 4 for detailed content requirements.

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Part 4 paragraph 39 - Requirement to have an appropriate policy document in place
sources.summary: The content requirement paragraph 5 points to: for any Part 2 condition (including paragraph 18's safeguarding condition), the policy document must describe Article 5 compliance procedures for that processing and set out retention/erasure policy including expected retention period.

sources.title: Online Safety Act 2023 section 3 - Meaning of "user-to-user service" and "search service"
sources.summary: Defines "user-to-user service" and "search service", the two categories Part 3 regulates, and the rule for classifying a combined service.

sources.title: Online Safety Act 2023 section 11 - Children's risk assessment duties
sources.summary: Requires providers of user-to-user services likely to be accessed by children to keep a current children's risk assessment covering primary priority, priority and non-designated content harmful to children.

sources.title: Online Safety Act 2023 section 12 - Safety duties protecting children
sources.summary: Requires proportionate systems, including age verification or estimation, to keep all children away from primary priority content and protect at-risk age groups from priority and non-designated harmful content.

sources.title: Online Safety Act 2023 section 20 - Duty about content reporting
sources.summary: Requires accessible reporting systems for illegal content and, for services likely accessed by children, content harmful to children. "Affected persons" includes a parent or guardian of a child user. Subsections (1)-(6),(7)(a) in force; (7)(b) unconfirmed.

sources.title: Online Safety Act 2023 section 21 - Duties about complaints procedures
sources.summary: Requires transparent complaints procedures covering illegal content and content harmful to children. Subsections (1)-(5),(6)(a)(b)(d)(e),(7),(8),(9)(a) in force; remainder unconfirmed.

sources.title: Online Safety Act 2023 section 35 - Children's access assessments
sources.summary: Requires an evidence-based assessment of whether children access the service. Subsection (2): a provider may only conclude children cannot access a service if age verification or estimation is used to that effect - self-declaration does not qualify.

sources.title: Online Safety Act 2023 section 36 - Duties about children's access assessments
sources.summary: Requires an initial children's access assessment within the Schedule 3 timeframe, repeated at least yearly and after significant change.

sources.title: Online Safety Act 2023 section 37 - Meaning of "likely to be accessed by children"
sources.summary: Defines the trigger for Part 3's children's duties: the provider's own s.35 assessment, a failed mandatory assessment, or an OFCOM determination.

sources.title: Online Safety Act 2023 section 55 - Meaning of "regulated user-generated content", "user-generated content", "news publisher content"
sources.summary: Core Part 3 interpretation section defining user-generated content (with email/SMS/one-to-one carve-outs) and news publisher content.

sources.title: Online Safety Act 2023 section 61 - Primary priority content that is harmful to children
sources.summary: Sets the statutory primary-priority-content categories directly in the Act: pornographic content (text-only carve-out) and content promoting suicide, self-harm or eating disorders. This is what s.12 requires keeping all children away from.

sources.title: Online Safety Act 2023 section 66 - Requirement to report CSEA content to the NCA
sources.summary: Requires providers to detect and report child sexual exploitation and abuse content to the National Crime Agency. User-to-user duty (1)-(2) and (7)-(10) in force since 7 April 2026; search-service duty (3)-(6) not yet in force.

sources.title: Online Safety Act 2023 Schedule 1 - Exempt user-to-user and search services
sources.summary: Exemptions list (not a category list): email, SMS/MMS, one-to-one live communications, limited-functionality and internal business services, public bodies, and eligible education/childcare providers.

sources.title: Online Safety Act 2023 section 214A - Power to require providers of internet services to prevent or restrict access by children to internet services
sources.summary: Delegated power (inserted 29 April 2026 by Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026 ss.70(2)/78(1)(b)) letting the Secretary of State make future regulations restricting children's access (time limits, curfews, stranger-contact restrictions). The power itself is in force; no regulations have been made under it yet (expected ~Spring 2027), so it currently creates no operative provider duty.

sources.title: Children Act 1989 section 2 - Parental responsibility for children
sources.summary: Who automatically holds parental responsibility: married/civil-partnered parents jointly, or the mother alone (father/second parent can acquire it later). More than one person can hold it at once; it cannot be surrendered, only delegated in its exercise.

sources.title: Children Act 1989 section 3 - Meaning of "parental responsibility"
sources.summary: Defines parental responsibility as all rights, duties, powers, responsibilities and authority a parent has towards a child and their property. Subsection (5): someone without parental responsibility but with care of the child may do what is reasonable to safeguard/promote welfare.

sources.title: Children Act 2004 section 11 - Arrangements to safeguard and promote welfare
sources.summary: Requires NAMED PUBLIC BODIES (local authorities, NHS England, ICBs, NHS trusts, police, NCA, youth offending teams, prison/secure-centre governors etc) to have arrangements ensuring their functions have regard to safeguarding children's welfare. A private company is not on the named-bodies list.

sources.title: Family Law Reform Act 1969 section 8 - Consent by persons over 16 to surgical, medical and dental treatment
sources.summary: A 16/17 year old can give valid consent to their own surgical, medical or dental treatment as if an adult; a parent's consent is not additionally required. Sits alongside, not instead of, the separate Gillick-competence route for under-16s. It governs consent to treatment given to the treating clinician.

sources.citation: Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026, s. 70
sources.title: Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026 section 70 - Power to require providers of internet services to prevent or restrict access by children to internet services
sources.summary: The amending provision (2026 c.21, Royal Assent 29 April 2026) that inserts OSA 2023 s.214A. See osa-2023-s-214a for the current live text of what it inserts.

sources.citation: Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026, s. 72
sources.title: Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026 section 72 - Age of consent in relation to processing of a child's personal data: information society services
sources.summary: The amending provision (2026 c.21, Royal Assent 29 April 2026) that inserts UK GDPR Articles 8(2A)-(2B) and 8ZA. See uk-gdpr-art-008 and uk-gdpr-art-008za for the current live text of what it inserts.

sources.title: Crime and Policing Act 2026 section 85 - Duty to report suspected child sex offences
sources.summary: Duty on adults (18+) carrying out a "relevant activity" involving children in England to notify police/local authority "as soon as practicable" on becoming aware of a suspected child sex offence. Implements an IICSA recommendation. Not yet commenced (s.255(1) default; not in either commencement SI made so far).

sources.title: Crime and Policing Act 2026 section 92 - Preventing or deterring a person from complying with duty to report suspected child sex offence
sources.summary: Obstruction offence: intentionally preventing/deterring a person from complying with the s.85 duty. Triable either way, up to 7 years on indictment. Failure to report itself is deliberately not criminalised. Not yet commenced, same basis as s.85.

sources.title: Age appropriate design: a code of practice for online services (ICO Children's code)
sources.summary: The statutory Children's code (DPA 2018 s.123) and its 15 standards for online services likely to be accessed by children: best interests, DPIA, age-appropriate application, transparency, no detrimental use, policy adherence, high-privacy defaults, data minimisation, no unwarranted sharing, geolocation off by default, parental controls transparency, profiling off by default, no nudge techniques, connected-toy conformance, and accessible rights tools.

sources.citation: ICO Children and the UK GDPR
sources.title: Children and the UK GDPR
