sources.summary: ICO's operative guidance on Article 8 age-of-consent mechanics, the preventive/counselling exception, the 4-part 'offering an ISS directly to a child' test, Gillick competence for services not offered directly to children, a child's own capacity to exercise data protection rights, and the 'likely to be accessed by children' test. Last updated 15 May 2026 to reflect the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.

sources.citation: ICO Age assurance for the Children's code
sources.title: Age assurance for the Children's code
sources.summary: Commissioner's Opinion (18 January 2024, replacing the October 2021 version) on acceptable age assurance methods: self-declaration is inadequate for high-risk processing but may suit low-risk or combined use; proportionality guidance against infeasible or disproportionate methods; and how the Children's code runs in parallel with, not as a substitute for, Online Safety Act age-assurance duties. ICO flags this opinion itself as under DUAA-driven review with no replacement text published yet.

sources.title: Safeguarding Vulnerable Groups Act 2006 section 6 - Regulated activity providers
sources.summary: Who is a regulated activity provider: a person responsible for the management or control of regulated activity, not supervised in that responsibility, who makes or authorises arrangements for another person to engage in it. Private arrangements by an individual are excluded. Whether a person falls inside this section decides whether it carries the provider duties in Part 1.

sources.title: Safeguarding Vulnerable Groups Act 2006 section 36 - Personnel suppliers: duty to refer
sources.summary: A personnel supplier that is an employment agency or employment business must give the DBS prescribed information about a person it acts for when it stops acting for them, or would have, because it thinks Schedule 3 paragraph 1, 2, 7 or 8 applies, they have engaged in relevant conduct under paragraph 4 or 10, or the harm test is met. Subsection (7) defines when an agency acts for a person: arrangements with a view to finding them employment or supplying them to employers.

sources.title: Safeguarding Vulnerable Groups Act 2006 section 60 - Interpretation
sources.summary: Definitions for the Act, including child (under 18), vulnerable adult, DBS, and personnel supplier, which means a person carrying on an employment agency or employment business within the meaning of the Employment Agencies Act 1973, or an educational institution supplying students for experience of regulated activity.

sources.title: Safeguarding Vulnerable Groups Act 2006 Schedule 3 paragraph 1 - Automatic inclusion in the children's barred list
sources.summary: Automatic barring without representations: where a prescribed criterion is met, the DBS must include the person in the children's barred list. One of the four grounds section 36(4)(a) names for a personnel supplier's duty to refer.

sources.title: Safeguarding Vulnerable Groups Act 2006 Schedule 3 paragraph 2 - Inclusion in the children's barred list subject to representations
sources.summary: Automatic barring with representations: where a prescribed criterion is met and the person is, has been or might be engaged in regulated activity relating to children, the DBS must invite representations and then include the person in the children's barred list. One of the grounds section 36(4)(a) names.

sources.title: Safeguarding Vulnerable Groups Act 2006 Schedule 3 paragraph 4 - Relevant conduct in relation to children
sources.summary: Defines relevant conduct for the children's barred list: conduct that endangers or is likely to endanger a child, conduct involving sexual material relating to children, sexually explicit violent images, and inappropriate conduct of a sexual nature involving a child. Section 36(4)(b) makes this one of the grounds for a personnel supplier's duty to refer.

sources.title: Safeguarding Vulnerable Groups Act 2006 Schedule 3 paragraph 7 - Automatic inclusion in the adults' barred list
sources.summary: Automatic barring without representations for the adults' barred list, mirroring paragraph 1. One of the grounds section 36(4)(a) names for a personnel supplier's duty to refer.

sources.title: Safeguarding Vulnerable Groups Act 2006 Schedule 3 paragraph 8 - Inclusion in the adults' barred list subject to representations
sources.summary: Automatic barring with representations for the adults' barred list, mirroring paragraph 2. One of the grounds section 36(4)(a) names.

sources.title: Safeguarding Vulnerable Groups Act 2006 Schedule 3 paragraph 10 - Relevant conduct in relation to vulnerable adults
sources.summary: Defines relevant conduct for the adults' barred list, mirroring paragraph 4 for vulnerable adults. Section 36(4)(b) makes this one of the grounds for a personnel supplier's duty to refer.

sources.title: Employment Agencies Act 1973 section 6 - Restriction on charging persons seeking employment, etc.
sources.summary: A person carrying on an employment agency must not request or receive, directly or indirectly, any fee from a person for services for the purpose of finding that person employment, except in cases the Secretary of State prescribes. Contravention is an offence.

sources.title: Employment Agencies Act 1973 section 13 - Interpretation
sources.summary: Definitions that decide whether the Act applies: employment includes engagement under a contract for services; an employment agency is the business of providing services, whether by information or otherwise, for finding persons employment with employers or supplying employers with persons; an employment business is the business of participating in employment arrangements. Subsection (4) excludes publishing and advertising display, and subsection (7) lists the bodies the Act does not apply to.

sources.title: Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 regulation 26 - Circumstances in which fees may be charged to work-seekers
sources.summary: The only cases in which section 6(1)(a) of the 1973 Act does not apply: an agency finding a work-seeker employment in one of the occupations listed in Schedule 3, with the fee payable out of earnings, and not at all where the agency also charges the hirer for the same introduction. Confirms the fee ban applies everywhere outside those occupations.

sources.title: Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 Schedule 3 - Occupations in respect of which employment agencies may charge fees to work-seekers
sources.summary: The closed list of occupations regulation 26 exempts from the work-seeker fee ban: performers and production roles in the entertainment industry, photographic or fashion models and professional sports persons. Counselling and psychotherapy are not on it.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 10 - Processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences
sources.summary: Personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences may be processed under Article 6(1) only under the control of official authority or where domestic law authorises it with appropriate safeguards; a comprehensive register of convictions may be kept only under official authority. A DBS, PVG or AccessNI result, including a clear one, is Article 10 data; processing it needs both an Article 6 basis and a DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Part 1, 2 or 3 condition through section 10(5).

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Part 1 paragraph 1 - Employment, social security and social protection
sources.summary: Part 1 condition: processing necessary to perform or exercise obligations or rights imposed or conferred by law on the controller or data subject in connection with employment, social security or social protection, with an appropriate policy document in place. Available for a criminal-record check only where a legal obligation attaches to the engagement, which excludes most self-employed engagements.

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Part 2 paragraph 6 - Statutory etc and government purposes
sources.summary: Part 2 condition: processing necessary for the exercise of a function conferred on a person by an enactment or rule of law, or a function of the Crown, a Minister or a government department, and necessary for reasons of substantial public interest. Paragraph 36 removes the substantial-public-interest limb when the condition is used for criminal offence data.

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Part 2 paragraph 10 - Preventing etc unlawful acts
sources.summary: Part 2 condition: processing necessary for the prevention, investigation or detection of an unlawful act, which must be carried out without the data subject's consent so as not to prejudice those purposes, and necessary for reasons of substantial public interest. The ICO's own DBS example names this condition; a barred person engaging in regulated activity with children commits an offence under SVGA 2006 section 7, so a barred-list check can fall within it, read with paragraph 36.

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Part 2 paragraph 11 - Protecting the public against dishonesty etc
sources.summary: Part 2 condition: processing necessary for the exercise of a protective function, carried out without consent so as not to prejudice that function, and necessary for reasons of substantial public interest. A protective function is one intended to protect the public against dishonesty, malpractice, incompetence, unfitness, mismanagement or failures in services. Read with paragraph 36 for criminal offence data.

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Part 2 paragraph 17 - Counselling etc
sources.summary: Part 2 condition: processing necessary for the provision of confidential counselling, advice or support or another similar confidential service, carried out without consent because consent cannot be given, cannot reasonably be obtained, or would prejudice the service, and necessary for reasons of substantial public interest. Bears on the under-18 map's preventive-or-counselling question and on holding a child's disclosure where guardian consent cannot be routed safely.

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Part 3 paragraph 29 - Consent
sources.summary: Part 3 condition: the data subject has given consent to the processing. The ICO's DBS guidance holds that consent an organisation requires before running a check is not freely given and cannot be withdrawn, so this condition is not available for a check that an organisation requires; the individual's authority is separately a Police Act 1997 section 116A precondition for an Update Service check.

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Part 3 paragraph 30 - Protecting individual's vital interests
sources.summary: Part 3 condition: processing necessary to protect the vital interests of an individual where the data subject is physically or legally incapable of giving consent. Mirrored for completeness of the Part 3 criminal-offence-data conditions.

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Part 3 paragraph 32 - Personal data in the public domain
sources.summary: Part 3 condition: the processing relates to personal data manifestly made public by the data subject. Mirrored for completeness of the Part 3 conditions; a DBS, PVG or AccessNI result is never manifestly public, so it does not apply to criminal-record check results.

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Part 3 paragraph 33 - Legal claims
sources.summary: Part 3 condition: processing necessary for legal proceedings including prospective proceedings, for obtaining legal advice, or otherwise for establishing, exercising or defending legal rights. It can support retaining a record of a decision after the processing that produced it, for a limitation period.

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Part 3 paragraph 36 - Extension of conditions in Part 2 referring to substantial public interest
sources.summary: Part 3 condition: the processing would meet a Part 2 condition but for that condition's express requirement that the processing be necessary for reasons of substantial public interest. Read with a Part 2 condition such as paragraph 18 (safeguarding of children) or paragraph 10 (preventing unlawful acts), it removes the substantial-public-interest limb for criminal offence data.

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Part 3 paragraph 37 - Extension of insurance conditions
sources.summary: Part 3 condition: processing that would meet the paragraph 20 insurance condition, or paragraph 36 by virtue of it, but for the requirement that the data be of the specified special categories. It applies to processing for insurance purposes.

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Part 4 paragraph 38 - Application of this Part of this Schedule
sources.summary: Scope provision for Part 4: the appropriate policy document and additional safeguards in paragraphs 39 to 41 apply to processing carried out in reliance on any Part 1, 2 or 3 condition that requires an appropriate policy document. Paragraphs 18, 10 and 36 all carry that requirement, so Part 4 binds processing that relies on them.

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Part 4 paragraph 40 - Additional safeguard: retention of appropriate policy document
sources.summary: Where processing relies on a paragraph 38 condition, the controller must retain the appropriate policy document, review and update it, and make it available to the Commissioner on request, throughout the relevant period: from the start of the processing until six months after the processing ends. Sets the retention floor for an appropriate policy document.

sources.title: DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Part 4 paragraph 41 - Additional safeguard: record of processing
sources.summary: Where processing relies on a paragraph 38 condition, the Article 30 record of processing must state which condition is relied on, how the processing satisfies Article 6, and whether personal data is retained and erased in accordance with the policy document, with reasons for any departure. Read with UK GDPR Article 30(5), which removes the small-organisation exemption for Article 10 data, this makes a record-of-processing entry for criminal-record processing mandatory.

sources.title: Police Act 1997 section 113A - Criminal record certificates
sources.summary: The standard criminal record certificate: the DBS must issue one on an application countersigned by a registered person who states the certificate is required for the purposes of an exempted question, and the certificate gives prescribed details of every relevant matter on central records or states there is none. Establishes what a certificate is and that the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974 exempted question is the gateway to it. Note: legislation.gov.uk serves the England and Wales and Northern Ireland extent versions on one page; Part V is repealed for Scotland from 1 April 2025.

sources.title: Police Act 1997 section 113B - Enhanced criminal record certificates
sources.summary: The enhanced criminal record certificate: issued on an application countersigned by a registered person who states it is required for the purposes of an exempted question asked for a prescribed purpose, carrying central-record matters plus any information a chief officer reasonably believes relevant and ought to be included. Subsection (2)(b)'s prescribed purposes, set by regulation 5A of the 2002 Regulations, decide whether a role is eligible for the check, and section 116A(11) borrows the same test for who may receive Update Service information.

sources.title: Police Act 1997 section 116A - Up-date arrangements
sources.summary: The statutory footing of the DBS Update Service: the DBS may make arrangements for a certificate holder to subscribe so that a relevant person, authorised by the individual and seeking the information for the purposes of an exempted question asked for a prescribed purpose, can be told whether the certificate remains current. The certificate holder's authority is the precondition, and eligibility for the exempted question is the test for who may be the relevant person.

sources.title: Police Act 1997 section 124 - Offences: disclosure
sources.summary: A member, officer or employee of a registered body, or a person acting on their behalf, commits an offence by disclosing certificate or up-date information otherwise than in the course of their duties to another person entitled to it or with the applicant's consent; a fine on summary conviction. Drives the DBS handling guidance's access-controlled storage and its record of everyone to whom certificate information is revealed.

sources.title: Police Act 1997 (Criminal Records) Regulations 2002 regulation 5A - Enhanced criminal record certificates: prescribed purposes
sources.summary: Prescribes, for Police Act 1997 section 113B(2)(b), the purposes for which a registered person may state that an enhanced certificate is required, including considering an applicant's suitability for regulated activity relating to children and the other child-related circumstances the regulation cross-refers to. Together with the Exceptions Order this is what makes a self-employed counsellor who works with children eligible for an enhanced check with a children's barred-list check, and it is the same purpose test section 116A(11) applies to an Update Service recipient.

sources.title: Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974 (Exceptions) Order 1975 article 3 - Exceptions relating to questions and disclosure
sources.summary: Disapplies section 4(2) of the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974 so that a question about spent convictions may be asked, and must be answered, when assessing suitability for a profession, office, employment, work or occupation listed in Schedule 1. This is the 'exempted question' on which Police Act 1997 sections 113A, 113B and 116A all turn; whether a suitability question is one decides whether certificate or Update Service information may be sought at all.

sources.title: Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974 (Exceptions) Order 1975 Schedule 1 - Excepted professions, offices, employments, work and occupations
sources.summary: The list of excepted professions, offices, employments, work and occupations for which article 3 lifts the protection of spent convictions, including regulated activity relating to children and vulnerable adults and work in health and social care. Determines whether a therapist working with under-18s sits inside the exception, which is the precondition for an enhanced DBS check. Note: legislation.gov.uk serves this Schedule with its many extent-specific amendments on one page, so the mirrored body is long.

sources.title: SVGA 2006 section 7 - Barred person not to engage in regulated activity
sources.summary: An individual commits an offence by seeking, offering or engaging in regulated activity from which they are barred, punishable by up to five years' imprisonment on indictment. The offence a children's barred-list check is designed to prevent, and an unlawful act for the purposes of DPA 2018 Schedule 1 paragraph 10 (read with paragraph 36).

sources.title: SVGA 2006 section 9 - Use of barred person for regulated activity
sources.summary: A person commits an offence by permitting a barred individual to engage in regulated activity knowing or having reason to believe they are barred, and a personnel supplier commits an offence by supplying a barred individual to another who will arrange regulated activity, with the same knowledge. A barred-list check guards against this offence.

sources.title: Safeguarding Vulnerable Groups Act 2006 Schedule 4 paragraph 1 - Regulated activity: general
sources.summary: The general test for regulated activity relating to children: an activity in paragraph 2(1) carried out frequently by the same person, or on more than a set number of days in a 30-day period, or overnight, subject to the supervision exclusions and the establishment limb in sub-paragraph (2). Decides whether ongoing work with a child is regulated activity, which in turn decides eligibility for an enhanced check with a children's barred-list check.

sources.title: Safeguarding Vulnerable Groups Act 2006 Schedule 4 paragraph 2 - Activities
sources.summary: The list of activities that can be regulated activity relating to children, including any form of teaching, training or instruction, care or supervision, advice or guidance provided wholly or mainly for children relating to their physical, emotional or educational well-being, and health care. Counselling and psychotherapy for a child fall within the advice-or-guidance and health-care limbs.

sources.title: Safeguarding Vulnerable Groups Act 2006 Schedule 4 paragraph 3 - Establishments
sources.summary: The establishments in which work of any kind, done frequently or under the day-count test, is regulated activity relating to children: schools, children's homes, childcare premises and similar settings. Mirrored so the Part 1 definition is complete alongside paragraphs 1 and 2.

sources.title: PVG (Scotland) Act 2007 section 45A - Duration of Scheme membership
sources.summary: As substituted by the Disclosure (Scotland) Act 2020 from 1 April 2025: a scheme member participates in the Scheme for a type of regulated role for five years from joining, unless earlier removed, and membership may be renewed. Sets the recheck baseline for PVG scheme membership.

sources.title: PVG (Scotland) Act 2007 section 45C - Individuals must be scheme members to carry out regulated roles
sources.summary: From 1 April 2025 it is an offence for an individual to carry out, or agree to carry out, a regulated role with children or with adults without being a scheme member for that type of role. The Scottish counterpart to SVGA 2006 section 7 and the reason PVG membership is a mandatory condition for a counsellor working with children in Scotland.

sources.title: PVG (Scotland) Act 2007 section 45D - Organisations not to use individuals for regulated roles without confirming scheme membership
sources.summary: It is an offence for an organisation to offer a regulated role to, or use, an individual without first confirming that the individual is a scheme member for that type of role, with the confirmation routes the section describes. The Scottish counterpart to SVGA 2006 section 9.

sources.title: PVG (Scotland) Act 2007 section 45G - Penalties for offences relating to regulated roles by individuals not in Scheme
sources.summary: The penalties for offences under sections 45C to 45F: on summary conviction a fine or imprisonment, and on conviction on indictment up to five years, a fine or both. Mirrored so the Scottish offence provisions are complete.

sources.title: PVG (Scotland) Act 2007 section 46 - Confirmation of scheme membership
sources.summary: Ministers must provide a confirmation of scheme membership to each scheme member, stating the prescribed particulars of the membership and its type. The document a Scottish practitioner holds instead of a paper certificate, and the document a section 54 third-party confirmation reproduces.

sources.title: PVG (Scotland) Act 2007 section 54 - Provision of confirmation of scheme membership to third parties
sources.summary: Where a scheme member asks Ministers to make a confirmation of scheme membership available to a third party the member specifies, Ministers must comply. A section 54 third party need not be an accredited body, and it receives the confirmation of membership rather than a disclosure record.

sources.title: Disclosure (Scotland) Act 2020 Schedule 3 - Schedule to be substituted for Schedule 2 of the PVG Act (regulated roles with children)
sources.summary: The new Schedule 2 to the PVG (Scotland) Act 2007, in force from 1 April 2025, defining a regulated role with children as one that involves an activity in Part 2 and meets the Part 1 conditions. Part 2 paragraph 24 lists the counselling, advice and guidance activity that brings a therapist working with children inside the Scheme. legislation.gov.uk has no per-paragraph address for this Schedule, so the whole Schedule is mirrored in one entry.

sources.title: Criminal offence data
sources.summary: Curated from the three ICO pages 'What is criminal offence data?', 'What are the rules on criminal offence data?' and 'What are the conditions for processing?'. Settles that a DBS, PVG or AccessNI result is Article 10 criminal offence data even when it shows no convictions, so its holder needs both an Article 6 lawful basis and a DPA 2018 Schedule 1 condition. The ICO's own delivery-company example says consent to carry out a DBS check is not a valid Schedule 1 condition for a self-employed workforce and points to condition 10 (preventing or detecting unlawful acts); condition 18 (safeguarding) is the other fit, and paragraph 36 removes the substantial public interest test for criminal offence data. Both conditions require an appropriate policy document, a justification for not using consent, and a DPIA because the data determines access to an opportunity.

sources.citation: ICO employment practices guidance: pre-employment vetting of candidates
sources.title: Pre-employment vetting of candidates
sources.summary: Settles that criminal records vetting is only justified where the role carries an identified risk such as work with children, must be proportionate with no less intrusive alternative, and must never be applied routinely. The ICO names DBS, AccessNI and Disclosure Scotland as the only routes for conviction data, requires a DPIA, forbids forcing an individual to make a subject access request to the DBS, and requires a lawful basis plus a Schedule 1 condition. Vetting material must be destroyed as soon as reasonably practicable, keeping only a record of the outcome and decision. Still draft guidance at the time of curation.

sources.title: Revised Code of Practice for Disclosure and Barring Service Registered Persons
sources.summary: The statutory code issued under section 122 of the Police Act 1997 that binds every DBS registered body and every recipient of Update Service information under section 116A. It settles that a recipient of Update Service information must hold a written secure-handling policy and a written policy on the suitability of ex-offenders, must handle certificate information under data protection law, and commits an offence under section 124 if it discloses certificate content beyond entitled staff. It also fixes the legislative basis for enhanced checks with a barred list check and defines the umbrella function through which unregistered organisations obtain checks.

sources.citation: DBS Handling of certificate information (4 July 2018)
sources.title: Handling of DBS certificate information
sources.summary: The DBS sample policy on storage, handling, use, retention and disposal of certificate information. It settles the permitted record: no photocopy or image of a certificate, only the date of issue, subject name, type of certificate, position, unique reference number and the decision taken. Retention is no longer than necessary for disputes or safeguarding audits, with secure destruction afterwards; the earlier six-month figure was removed in the 4 July 2018 revision and survives only in the UK Government Web Archive. Certificate information passes only to those authorised under section 124 of the Police Act 1997 and only for the purpose the applicant consented to.

sources.citation: DBS Update Service employer guide (28 August 2026)
sources.title: DBS Update Service employer guide
sources.summary: The DBS guide governing who may run a free online status check on a Standard or Enhanced certificate. It settles that a check requires the applicant's consent, a legal declaration under section 116A that the checker may ask an exempted question for the role, the same workforce and level, an identity check, and sight of the original paper certificate in person by the checker or the recruiting organisation (copies and video are not enough). It defines the four result strings, the 30 calendar day subscription window from the certificate issue date, the record an organisation may keep, and that any recruiting organisation accessing the information must follow the Code of Practice and hold an ex-offenders policy.

sources.citation: DBS Eligibility for Enhanced with Barred List DBS checks with children (1 September 2026)
sources.title: Eligibility for Enhanced with Barred List DBS checks with children
sources.summary: DBS guidance on which roles are regulated activity with children and so eligible for an Enhanced check with a Children's Barred List check. It settles that healthcare to a child, expressly including psychotherapy and counselling, is regulated activity on a single occasion with no period condition, and that advice or guidance on emotional wellbeing qualifies when the period condition is met. That places a therapist treating under-18s in the child workforce. The guidance applies to paid and unpaid roles and is silent on self-employed applicants.

sources.title: AccessNI Code of Practice
sources.summary: The section 122 Police Act 1997 Code binding AccessNI Registered Bodies and other recipients of disclosure information in Northern Ireland. It settles that a recipient that is not a Registered Body is outside the Code's formal scope but that section 124 makes onward disclosure of certificate content an offence for any recipient. It fixes the handling standard: retain nothing longer than the suitability decision needs, keep a written secure-handling policy and a written ex-offender suitability policy, tell applicants in advance, discuss disclosed content before withdrawing an offer, and never reproduce a result as if it were a certificate. Annex A confirms criminal offence data needs a lawful basis plus an additional DPA 2018 condition.

sources.citation: AccessNI Guidance for Individuals Viewing Self-Employed Workers or Personal Employees AccessNI Checks (February 2026)
sources.title: Guide for viewing self-employed workers and personal employees' checks
sources.summary: AccessNI's guidance for anyone engaging a self-employed worker or personal employee in Northern Ireland. It settles that the worker applies for their own enhanced check through an AccessNI Umbrella Body, that the only acceptable evidence is the digital certificate shared from the worker's AccessNI account, and that copies or photographs must be rejected. The share link arrives by email, stays live for five calendar days and can be viewed once. The viewer checks identity, barred-list groups, disclosed content and issue date, uses the information for one suitability decision only, shares it with no third party and keeps no copy or representation of the contents.

sources.title: PECR regulation 2 - Interpretation
sources.summary: PECR's interpretation provision. Since 20 August 2025 it carries the operative definition of 'direct marketing': the communication (by whatever means) of advertising or marketing material which is directed to particular individuals, inserted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 section 110(2)(c) and identical to DPA 2018 section 122(5). Also defines 'electronic mail', 'individual', 'corporate subscriber' and 'consent' (which tracks the UK GDPR meaning). The first stop for whether a message is direct marketing at all.

sources.title: Medical Devices Regulations 2002 regulation 2 - Interpretation
sources.summary: The medical devices interpretation provision, carried as separately labelled Great Britain and Northern Ireland versions. The Great Britain definition of 'medical device' turns on the purpose the manufacturer intends: an instrument, apparatus, appliance, software or other article intended for diagnosis, prevention, monitoring, treatment or alleviation of disease, among other medical purposes. The first stop for whether a software feature, such as a patient-specific suggestion, gives a product a medical purpose.

sources.title: DPA 2018 section 122 - Direct marketing code
sources.summary: Requires the Commissioner to prepare a direct marketing code of practice, and in subsection (5) supplies the statutory definition of 'direct marketing' that PECR regulation 2 now repeats: the communication (by whatever means) of advertising or marketing material which is directed to particular individuals. In force since 25 May 2018; DUAA 2025 did not amend it, and the pending S.I. 2026/386 substitutions are wording changes only.

sources.citation: ICO direct marketing guidance: identify direct marketing
sources.title: Direct marketing guidance: identify direct marketing
sources.summary: The ICO's step-one test for whether a communication is direct marketing. Breaks the statutory definition into its three limbs, defines 'direct marketing purposes' (including consent-seeking messages), and sets the service-message boundary: an administrative or customer-service message is not direct marketing, but a service message carrying any promotional element becomes direct marketing even where promotion is not its main purpose. Tone, phrasing and context decide borderline cases; general branding or logos do not.

sources.citation: ICO guidance on direct marketing using electronic mail: key concepts
sources.title: Guidance on direct marketing using electronic mail: key concepts
sources.summary: The ICO's detailed electronic mail guidance, updated 28 April 2026 for DUAA 2025. Restates the direct marketing definition, confirms that purely administrative service messages fall outside it and that adding advertising or marketing material brings a message back inside, and defines 'electronic mail' to include email, SMS, in-app messages and social media direct messages but not display or feed adverts. Also distinguishes solicited from unsolicited marketing and individual from corporate subscribers.

sources.citation: ICO Guide to PECR: electronic mail marketing
sources.title: Guide to PECR: electronic mail marketing
sources.summary: The Guide to PECR's brief statement of the regulation 22 rules: no electronic mail marketing to individuals without specific consent, the existing-customer 'soft opt-in' and its opt-out conditions, the broad meaning of 'electronic mail', the identity and contact-address requirements, the viral marketing prohibition and the compliance checklist. Carries the ICO's notice that the Guide is under review following DUAA 2025.

sources.title: Consent
sources.summary: Curated from 'What is valid consent?', 'When is consent appropriate?' and 'How should we obtain, record and manage consent?'. Covers the Article 4(11) definition, freely given (no bundling, imbalance of power), specific and informed, clear affirmative action, explicit consent in a clear statement naming the special category data, consent from people in vulnerable situations, research consent and withdrawal, the invalidity checklist, the four records that demonstrate consent, and withdrawal as easy as giving consent.

sources.title: Anonymisation
sources.summary: Curated from 'Introduction to anonymisation', 'How do we ensure anonymisation is effective?' and 'Pseudonymisation'. Anonymisation reduces identification risk to a sufficiently remote level; identifiability is a spectrum judged by means reasonably likely to be used (Recital 26), assessed in whose hands the data sits; the motivated intruder test and its assumed capabilities and motivations; pseudonymised data stays personal data for anyone holding the additional information; DPA 2018 s.171 re-identification offences.

sources.title: Special category data
sources.summary: Curated from 'What is special category data?', 'What are the rules on special category data?' and 'What are the conditions for processing?'. Health data definition and scope, inferred special category data, the need for both an Article 6 basis and an Article 9 condition, the meaning of 'necessary', mandatory DPIA triggers, explicit consent, the Article 9(2)(h) health or social care condition with its confidentiality safeguard and the s.204 list of health professionals (which names child psychotherapists and arts therapists), and the Article 9(2)(j) research condition.

sources.citation: ICO guidance on AI and data protection
sources.title: Guidance on AI and data protection
sources.summary: Curated from 'What are the accountability and governance implications of AI?' and 'How do we ensure lawfulness in AI?'. Most AI use will need a DPIA; what an AI DPIA must describe, including human involvement and allocative and representational harms; necessity, proportionality and trade-offs; residual risk and prior consultation; controller decisions in AI supply chains; separate lawful bases for development and deployment; consent for AI; and when AI inferences are special category data.

sources.title: Data protection impact assessments (DPIAs)
sources.summary: Curated from 'What is a DPIA?', 'When do we need to do a DPIA?' and 'How do we do a DPIA?'. The Article 35(1) rule, the three Article 35(3) mandatory cases, the nine WP29 indicators (two usually trigger a DPIA), the ICO Article 35(4) list including innovative technology such as AI, vulnerable individuals, large scale (individual professionals processing client data are not large scale), exceptions, the seven-step process, and sign-off, residual risk and review.

sources.citation: MHRA Medical device stand-alone software including apps (v1.10f)
sources.title: MHRA: Medical device stand-alone software including apps
sources.summary: MHRA guidance on when stand-alone software and apps qualify as medical devices in Great Britain. Qualification follows the intended purpose read objectively from labelling, instructions and promotional material, and a general 'not a medical device' disclaimer does not cure a medical claim made elsewhere. Decision support is unlikely to be a device where options are explained but a professional decides, or where it offers only lifestyle choices or referral advice; it is likely to be one where it influences the actual treatment. Treatment recommendations for listed conditions may be a device; reference information and signposting are unlikely to be.

sources.citation: MHRA Digital mental health technology: qualification and classification (Version 1.3)
sources.title: MHRA: Digital mental health technology qualification and classification
sources.summary: MHRA guidance for mental health software. A product has a medical purpose when it performs a clinical task, such as recommending therapeutic options, and targets conditions or symptoms at a diagnosable or clinically relevant level; healthcare administration support alone has none. A product with a medical purpose is software as a medical device when its functionality is high, which includes personalised output and AI processing. The first stop for whether a conversational feature that suggests therapy to one person has a medical purpose.

sources.citation: CAP Code Scope of the Code
sources.title: CAP Code: Scope of the Code
sources.summary: The CAP Code's remit: it covers marketing communications on a marketer's own website or other non-paid-for online space under its control that are directly connected with the supply of goods or services, and it excludes private correspondence with customers about existing relationships, editorial content and other website content outside that remit. The first stop for whether in-product copy is advertising at all.

sources.title: CAP Code Section 3: Misleading advertising
sources.summary: CAP Code section 3 general rules against materially misleading marketing communications, omission of material information, the substantiation duty, qualification of claims and exaggeration, the prices rules (3.17 to 3.22: no misleading price statements, non-optional charges included, the extent of a linked commitment stated) and the "free" rules (3.23 to 3.26: nothing to pay beyond the unavoidable cost of responding, the commitment made clear, no free element already in the package price, no "free trial" needing a non-refundable purchase), plus the endorsements and testimonials rules: no trust mark, quality mark or equivalent without authorisation and no false claim of approval, endorsement or authorisation by a public or private body (rule 3.52), no false code-of-conduct claims (3.53) and the asterisk that marks a rule as a practice unfair in all circumstances.

sources.citation: CAP Code s.12 Medicines, medical devices, health-related products and beauty products
sources.title: CAP Code Section 12: Medicines, medical devices, health-related products and beauty products
sources.summary: CAP Code section 12 rules requiring objective health claims to be backed by evidence, barring discouragement of essential medically-supervised treatment, and prohibiting false claims to prevent or treat disease, plus the section's definition of disease, the rule 12.12 prescription-only advertising restriction and the homeopathic scope of rule 12.20.

sources.citation: CAP AdviceOnline - Mental Health: Treatment claims
sources.title: Mental Health: Treatment claims
sources.summary: CAP Executive AdviceOnline guidance on advertising mental-health treatment claims: objective claims must be substantiated under Rule 12.1, and treatment, diagnosis or advice for serious medical conditions may only be advertised under the supervision of a suitably qualified medical professional. Last updated 15 Jul 2021.

sources.citation: CAP AdviceOnline - Health: Therapies and references to Medical Conditions
sources.title: Health: Therapies and references to Medical Conditions
sources.summary: CAP Executive AdviceOnline guidance on referencing medical conditions in therapy advertising: a claim that a therapy can diagnose, treat, help with or cure a medical condition needs suitable qualification and robust evidence under Rules 12.1 and 12.2, with worked before/after examples. Last updated 01 Sep 2022.

sources.title: Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 Schedule 2
sources.summary: Controlled-drug classifications under the 1971 Act, including the Class A list.

sources.title: Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001 Schedule 1
sources.summary: Drugs specified in Schedule 1 of the 2001 Regulations.

sources.title: Serious Crime Act 2007 section 44
sources.summary: The offence of intentionally encouraging or assisting an offence, including the intent requirement.

sources.title: Data Protection (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2017 section 2 - Application (Condition B, territorial scope)
sources.summary: The Guernsey Law applies to processing by a controller or processor established in the Bailiwick, or to processing of a Bailiwick resident's personal data in the context of offering them goods or services or monitoring their behaviour in the Bailiwick.

sources.title: Data Protection (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2017 section 39 - Controllers and processors to be registered
sources.summary: A controller or processor established in the Bailiwick must not process personal data unless it is registered under Schedule 4 or exempt by regulations. Failure to comply is an offence.

sources.title: Data Protection (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2017 section 47 - Mandatory designation of a data protection officer
sources.summary: A controller and processor must jointly designate a data protection officer where processing is carried out by a public authority, or where core activities involve large-scale systematic monitoring of data subjects or large-scale processing of special category data.

sources.citation: Guernsey DPL 2017 Sch.2 Part III para.18
sources.title: Data Protection (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2017 Schedule 2 Part III paragraph 18 - Explicit consent (special category data)
sources.summary: Sets explicit consent as a condition for processing special category data: the data subject has given explicit consent to processing for the purpose for which it is processed.

sources.title: Data Protection (Jersey) Law 2018 Article 4 - Application (territorial scope and representative duty)
sources.summary: The Jersey Law applies to processing by controllers or processors established in Jersey, those using equipment in Jersey, and those outside Jersey offering goods or services to, or monitoring, persons in Jersey. A controller using equipment in Jersey must nominate a representative established in Jersey.

sources.title: Data Protection (Jersey) Law 2018 Schedule 2 Part 2 paragraph 6 - Consent (special category data)
sources.summary: Sets consent as a condition for processing personal data and special category data: the data subject has given explicit consent to the processing for one or more specific purposes.

sources.title: Data Protection (Jersey) Law 2018 Article 24 - Appointment of data protection officer
sources.summary: A controller and processor must appoint a data protection officer where processing is by a public authority, where core activities need regular and systematic large-scale monitoring of data subjects or large-scale processing of special category data, or where the relevant law requires it.

sources.citation: Jersey Data Protection Authority Law 2018 Art.17
sources.title: Data Protection Authority (Jersey) Law 2018 Article 17 - Registration
sources.summary: A controller or processor established in Jersey must not cause or permit personal data to be processed unless it is registered under Article 17 of the Data Protection Authority (Jersey) Law 2018.

sources.title: Data Protection (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2017 section 17 - Right to object to processing for direct marketing purposes
sources.summary: Where personal data is processed for direct marketing, the data subject may require the controller to stop. The controller must give notice of the processing and this right explicitly and separately, at or before its first communication, and must stop on a written objection.

sources.title: Data Protection (Jersey) Law 2018 Article 36 - Right to object to processing for direct marketing purposes
sources.summary: A data subject may object to processing for direct marketing. The controller must notify them of the processing and the right explicitly and separately, at or before its first communication, and must stop processing on written notice of objection, including by automated means for information society services.

sources.title: Payment Services Regulations 2017 regulation 2 - Interpretation
sources.summary: Definitions for the Payment Services Regulations 2017, including payment service, money remittance, payment transaction, payer, payee, funds and payment instrument. The starting point for whether a platform that touches a client's or a funder's money is carrying on a payment service.

sources.title: Payment Services Regulations 2017 regulation 38 - Notification of use of limited network exclusion
sources.summary: A provider relying on the limited network exclusion in Schedule 1 Part 2 paragraph 2(k) must notify the FCA once its payment transactions exceed 1 million euros over 12 months. Bears on any voucher or code that a network issues for use with its own practitioners.

sources.title: Payment Services Regulations 2017 Schedule 1 - Payment services
sources.summary: Part 1 lists the activities that are payment services, including money remittance and issuing payment instruments. Part 2 lists the exclusions, including the commercial agent exclusion (paragraph 2(b)), technical service providers that never possess the funds (2(j)) and limited network instruments (2(k)).

sources.title: Electronic Money Regulations 2011 regulation 2 - Interpretation
sources.summary: Definitions for the Electronic Money Regulations 2011. Electronic money must be accepted by a person other than its issuer, so a prepaid credit that only the issuing platform accepts is not electronic money.

sources.title: Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 regulation 25 - Client accounts
sources.summary: An employment agency must not receive money on a work-seeker's behalf unless the money is remuneration in a Schedule 3 occupation and the agency keeps a client account under Schedule 2. Money from a hirer or a person connected with a hirer counts as received on the work-seeker's behalf.

sources.title: Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 regulation 2 - Interpretation
sources.summary: Definitions for the Conduct Regulations, including hirer, work-seeker, work-finding services and vulnerable person. A vulnerable person is any person who by reason of age, infirmity, illness, disability or any other circumstance is in need of care or attention, and includes any person under the age of eighteen; the definition controls when regulations 19(2) and 22 apply.

sources.title: Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 regulation 6 - Restriction on detrimental action relating to work-seekers working elsewhere
sources.summary: An agency or employment business must not, by a contract term or otherwise, subject or threaten a work-seeker with any detriment because they terminated or gave notice to terminate their contract with it (6(1)(a)), and must not require the work-seeker to tell it, or a connected person, who their future employer is (6(1)(b)). Losing benefits under the ended contract, recovering losses from work agreed and not done, and a reasonable notice period are not a detriment (6(2)).

sources.title: Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 regulation 32 - Application of the Regulations to work-seekers who are incorporated
sources.summary: Applies the Regulations to a work-seeker that is a company and to the person it supplies to do the work. Under 32(9) the company and that person may agree to disapply paragraphs (1) to (8) by notice before introduction or supply, and the agency must tell the hirer. The opt-out does not apply where the work involves any vulnerable person (32(12)), and work-finding services must not be made conditional on it (32(13)). It reaches only the Regulations, not section 6 of the Employment Agencies Act 1973.

sources.title: Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 regulation 13 - Notification of charges and the terms of offers
sources.summary: On first offering a service to a work-seeker, an agency must state whether it is a work-finding service for which the Act prohibits a fee and, where other paid services or goods may be provided, the fee, payee, service, cancellation right and refund terms. A further notice is due when such fees are introduced or varied.

sources.title: Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 regulation 16 - Requirement to obtain agreement to terms with work-seekers and content of terms with work-seekers: Agencies
sources.summary: The agency terms-of-business duty since the 2010 renumbering (formerly regulation 14). Before first providing a work-finding service for which regulation 26(1) permits a fee, an agency must obtain the work-seeker's agreement to terms covering the services, its authority to act, client money, the fee and refunds, and notice to terminate. It is triggered only where a fee is permitted, so it does not attach to an occupation outside Schedule 3.

sources.title: Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 regulation 19 - Confirmation to be obtained about a work-seeker
sources.summary: An agency must not introduce a work-seeker to a position that involves working with, caring for or attending a vulnerable person without confirming the work-seeker's identity and the experience, training, qualifications and authorisation the hirer, the law or a professional body requires, and must confirm the work-seeker is willing to take the position.

sources.title: Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 regulation 20 - Steps to be taken for the protection of the work-seeker and the hirer
sources.summary: Before an introduction an agency must take reasonably practicable steps to make both parties aware of legal or professional-body requirements for the position and must make reasonably practicable enquiries that the engagement would not be detrimental to either. An agency that later learns a work-seeker is or may be unsuitable must tell the hirer.

sources.title: Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 regulation 22 - Additional requirements where professional qualifications or authorisation are required or where work-seekers are to work with vulnerable persons
sources.summary: For a position working with, caring for or attending a vulnerable person, an agency must also obtain copies of relevant qualifications or authorisations and two non-relative references, offer copies to the hirer and take other reasonably practicable steps to confirm suitability, or tell the hirer what it could not obtain.

sources.title: Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 regulation 29 - Records
sources.summary: An agency must keep records sufficient to show compliance, including the Schedule 4 particulars for each work-seeker application and the Schedule 5 particulars for each hirer application, for at least one year from creation and at least one year after it last provides services to the applicant. Electronic records are permitted; applications on which no action is taken are exempt.

sources.title: Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 Schedule 4 - Particulars to be included in an agency's or employment business's records relating to work-seekers
sources.summary: The work-seeker record: name and address, the terms and any variation, training, experience, qualifications and authorisations with copies of evidence, the hirers the work-seeker is introduced to, any resulting engagement, fee requests and receipts where fees are permitted, and details of enquiries under regulations 19, 20 and 22.

sources.title: Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 Schedule 5 - Particulars to be included in an agency's or employment business's records relating to hirers
sources.summary: The hirer record: the position sought, its likely duration, the experience, qualifications and authorisation it requires, details of enquiries under regulations 18 and 20, and dates of fee requests and receipts from the hirer with copies of statements or invoices.

sources.title: Charities Act 2011 section 2 - Meaning of charitable purpose
sources.summary: A charitable purpose must fall within a description in section 3(1) and be for the public benefit. England and Wales only.

sources.title: Charities Act 2011 section 3 - Descriptions of purposes
sources.summary: The descriptions of charitable purposes, including the advancement of health (which includes the relief of human suffering) and the relief of those in need because of ill-health, financial hardship or other disadvantage.

sources.title: Charities Act 2011 section 4 - The public benefit requirement
sources.summary: No purpose is presumed to be for the public benefit; public benefit has the meaning given by the law of charities in England and Wales.

sources.title: Charities Act 2011 section 17 - Guidance as to operation of public benefit requirement
sources.summary: The Charity Commission publishes public benefit guidance, and charity trustees must have regard to it when exercising any power or duty to which it is relevant. Gives PB1 and PB2 their weight.

sources.title: Charities Act 1992 section 58 - Interpretation of Part II
sources.summary: Defines commercial participator and professional fundraiser. A business becomes a commercial participator when, in a promotional venture, it represents that charitable contributions will be given to or applied for a charitable institution.

sources.title: Charities Act 1992 section 59 - Prohibition on professional fund-raiser etc. raising funds for charitable institutions without an agreement in prescribed form
sources.summary: A commercial participator must not represent that charitable contributions will go to a charitable institution unless it acts under an agreement with the institution that meets the prescribed requirements.

sources.title: Charities Act 1992 section 60 - Professional fund-raisers etc. required to indicate institutions benefiting and arrangements for remuneration
sources.summary: The statement a professional fundraiser or commercial participator must give with a representation: the institutions that benefit and the notifiable amount of what they will receive.

sources.title: DPA 2018 section 121 - Data-sharing code
sources.summary: The Commissioner must prepare a code of practice on the sharing of personal data. The statutory footing of the ICO data sharing code.

sources.title: DPA 2018 section 204 - Meaning of health professional and social work professional
sources.summary: The closed list of health professionals and social work professionals for the DPA 2018, which section 11(1)(a) relies on for the Article 9(3) safeguard. Counsellors and psychotherapists registered only with BACP, NCPS or UKCP are not on it.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 29 - Processing under the authority of the controller or processor
sources.summary: A processor, and any person acting under the authority of the controller or processor who has access to personal data, must process it only on the controller's instructions unless domestic law requires otherwise.

sources.citation: FCA Handbook PERG 15.5: Negative scope/exclusions (Payment Services Regulations 2017)
sources.title: PERG 15.5 Negative scope/exclusions
sources.summary: FCA perimeter guidance on activities excluded from the Payment Services Regulations 2017. Covers platforms that collect and remit funds, the commercial agent exclusion and the authority it needs, escrow, online fundraising platforms passing on charitable donations and the limited network exclusion, including why online marketplaces are unlikely to qualify.

sources.citation: Charity Commission guidance PB1: Public benefit: the public benefit requirement
sources.title: Public benefit: the public benefit requirement (PB1)
sources.summary: The Charities Act public benefit requirement and its benefit and public aspects. Covers the bar on purposes that exclude the poor, the rule against named beneficiaries and the rule that personal or private benefit to an individual or organisation must be incidental to the purpose.

sources.citation: Charity Commission guidance PB2: Public benefit: running a charity
sources.title: Public benefit: running a charity (PB2)
sources.summary: The trustees' duty to carry out their charity's purposes for the public benefit when running it. Covers the range of proper decisions, charging for services without excluding the poor, provision for the poor that is more than minimal or token and keeping personal benefit incidental.

sources.citation: Charity Commission guidance CC3: The essential trustee: what you need to know, what you need to do
sources.title: The essential trustee: what you need to know, what you need to do (CC3)
sources.summary: The main legal duties of charity trustees. Covers carrying out the charity's purposes for the public benefit, the risk of personal reimbursement for spending on the wrong purposes, balanced and informed best-interests decisions, trustee benefit and conflicts of interest, income generation and personal liability.

sources.citation: Charity Commission guidance CC20: Charity fundraising: a guide to trustee duties
sources.title: Charity fundraising: a guide to trustee duties (CC20)
sources.summary: Trustee duties when a charity fundraises. Covers the professional fundraiser and commercial participator definitions, checking how much the charity gets compared with the amount generated overall, the mandatory written agreement before fundraising begins, solicitation statements and fundraising by trustees or connected people.

sources.citation: ICO Data sharing: a code of practice (DPA 2018 s.121)
sources.title: Data sharing: a code of practice
sources.summary: The ICO statutory code under DPA 2018 s.121, which the Commissioner and the courts must take into account (s.127). It covers sharing between separate or joint controllers but not access given to employees, contractors or processors, treats giving a third party access through your IT systems as sharing, and recommends a data sharing agreement that names the controllers, the lawful basis, special category conditions, individual rights, retention and termination.

sources.citation: ICO UK GDPR guidance: What does it mean if you are joint controllers?
sources.title: What does it mean if you are joint controllers?
sources.summary: Joint controllers share the same purposes, so controllers processing the same data for different purposes are not joint controllers. Joint controllers need no contract but must have a transparent arrangement whose main points are made available to individuals, each remains liable for the whole damage and individuals can exercise their rights against each one.

sources.citation: ICO UK GDPR guidance: Controllers and processors
sources.title: Controllers and processors
sources.summary: Curated from 'What are controllers and processors?', 'How do you determine whether you are a controller or processor?' and the brief guide's indicator checklists. Processors serve the controller's interests and cannot take overarching decisions such as what data to collect, providers acting under their own professional obligations are always controllers, a processor acting outside instructions becomes a controller and the checklists give indicators for controller, joint controller and processor.

sources.title: CMA207 - Unfair commercial practices: guidance on the unfair commercial practices provisions of the DMCC Act 2024
sources.summary: CMA guidance on the unfair commercial practices provisions of the DMCC Act 2024. The Schedule 20 practices are unfair in all circumstances with no need to show an effect on consumers, including displaying a trust mark, quality mark or equivalent without authorisation (banned practice 3) and falsely claiming approval, endorsement or authorisation by a public or private body (banned practice 4). Also covers the section 226 misleading actions on sponsorship, approval, affiliations or connections and on confusion with another trader's name or mark.

sources.citation: CMA compliance advice on urgency and price reduction claims (29 March 2023)
sources.title: Urgency claims and price reduction claims: compliance advice for online businesses
sources.summary: CMA open letter and examples on price reduction claims, meaning any discount or special offer price that refers to a higher comparison price. The higher price must be a genuine and realistic selling price that the trader can demonstrate and keep records for; a comparison with a price that is no longer, or never was, the product's usual selling price is likely to mislead, even when the words are literally true.

sources.citation: GOV.UK, Tutoring services: guidance for complying with Fair Work Agency (FWA) legislation (updated 7 April 2026)
sources.title: Tutoring services: guidance for complying with Fair Work Agency (FWA) legislation
sources.summary: FWA guidance for tutoring services. A service acting as an intermediary between people looking for work and a person or business looking for someone to do it is likely to be in scope of the Employment Agencies Act 1973 and the Conduct Regulations, whether private, public or not-for-profit. An agency introduces the worker to a hirer who contracts with them directly, and charging the worker a fee for work-finding services is a criminal offence.

sources.citation: GOV.UK, Overview of the Conduct Regulations 2003 (updated 22 June 2026)
sources.title: Overview of the Conduct Regulations 2003
sources.summary: FWA overview of the Act and the Conduct Regulations. The Act applies to a wide range of agencies, including online platforms; agencies must not charge workers fees for finding them work, but the Act does not regulate fees charged to hirers; other services unrelated to work-finding may be charged for; and a work-seeker cannot use the regulation 32(9) opt-out where the role involves working with vulnerable people.

sources.title: Employment agencies and businesses
sources.summary: GOV.UK guide for agencies and employment businesses. They cannot charge a work-seeker a fee for work-finding services, stop someone working elsewhere or make someone name a future employer. A publication or website totally or mostly aimed at providing a work-finding service will normally have to follow the rules, and limited-company workers cannot opt out where they will work with vulnerable people.

sources.title: Prices: General
sources.summary: CAP Executive advice on CAP Code rules 3.17 to 3.22. A "from" or "up to" price must not exaggerate availability: the ASA has regard to the CTSI pricing guidance, expects a significant proportion of items at the advertised price and judges what is significant case by case, and finds an unevidenced claim misleading. A "from £20/night" claim was substantiated by availability on 70% of days.
